proposedRecord.title: Guidelines: The Use of Artificial Intelligence by Judicial Officers
proposedRecord.description: Supreme Court of Victoria guidelines setting the parameters for use of artificial intelligence by the Court's own judicial officers, informed by the Victorian Law Reform Commission's eight principles.
proposedRecord.content: Dated 14 May 2026 and published in May 2026, these Guidelines outline the parameters around the use of artificial intelligence by judicial officers of the Supreme Court of Victoria. The Guidelines state that they have been informed by the eight principles formulated by the Victorian Law Reform Commission to guide the safe use of AI in courts and tribunals, set out in its report Artificial Intelligence in Victoria's Courts and Tribunals (October 2025). They define artificial intelligence for the purposes of the Guidelines and address how judicial officers may and may not use AI tools in the course of judicial work, including that judicial officers must not use GenAI for judicial decision-making (clause 3.1), that supportive uses are limited to tasks such as organising and locating case materials, producing summaries and chronologies, legal research and proof-reading (clauses 3.3 and 3.4), and that only AI tools approved by the Court are to be used with regard to confidentiality (clause 3.5). Clause 3.6 says judicial officers should give the staff assisting them clear directions on the appropriate use of AI and the level of disclosure the judicial officer requires. Clause 3.7 records that the Guidelines are intended to be reviewed as the technology and the Court's experience change. The Guidelines are published by the Supreme Court of Victoria as a downloadable document.

analysis.summary: PRACTICE NOTE Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen AI) Commencement 1. This Practice Note replaces the Practice Note that commenced on 3 February. It commences on 12 February 2025 and will apply to all proceedings from that date. Introduction 2. Generative AI ( Gen AI ) is a form of artificial intelligence that is capable of creating new content, including text, images or sounds, based on patterns and data acquired from a body of training material.

proposedRecord.title: Land and Environment Court Practice Note — Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen AI)
proposedRecord.description: Land and Environment Court of New South Wales practice note on generative AI, replacing its earlier note and adding an expert report transition requirement.
agencies: Land and Environment Court of New South Wales
proposedRecord.content: Issued by the Honourable Justice Brian J Preston, Chief Judge, on 11 February 2025, this Practice Note replaces the Court's earlier practice note that had commenced on 3 February 2025. It commences on 12 February 2025 and applies to all proceedings from that date. It identifies generative AI broadly across generic and legal-specific tools, and sets out the risks users must understand, including hallucinated citations and fabricated authorities, dependence on training data that may be inaccurate, out of date or not relevant to New South Wales, biased output, prompts being retained and reused, inadequate confidentiality and privilege safeguards, and training data obtained in breach of copyright. Information subject to non-publication or suppression orders, material produced on subpoena and material subject to a statutory prohibition upon publication must not be entered into any Gen AI program unless the legal practitioner or person responsible for the conduct of the proceeding is satisfied that the information will remain within the controlled environment of the platform and not be used to train any large language model, is used only in connection with the proceeding (unless otherwise required or permitted by law), and is not used to train the Gen AI program. Generative AI must not be used to generate the content of affidavits, witness statements, character references or other evidentiary material, nor to alter, embellish, strengthen, dilute or rephrase a witness's written evidence, with leave available in exceptional cases for attachments and annexures. Verification of authorities must not be carried out solely by using a generative AI tool. Paragraph 24 adds a transition requirement specific to this Court: expert reports prepared between the date the practice note was issued and the date it commenced must identify which part or parts of the report relied on generative AI in preparing its content. The practice note will be periodically reviewed.

proposedRecord.content: On 24 September 2026 the Prime Minister announced a Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet (PM&C)-led rapid review of whether existing legislative, governance and information-sharing arrangements are fit for purpose to prepare for and respond to cyber incidents involving artificial intelligence. PM&C published formal terms of reference the same day (https://www.pmc.gov.au/resources/terms-reference-rapid-review-australian-government-arrangements-ai-driven-cyber-incident; release date Thursday 24 September 2026). The review page states that PM&C leads the review in collaboration with the National Cyber Security Coordinator, the Australian Signals Directorate, the Australian AI Safety Institute and Services Australia. Per the terms of reference, recommendations scope covers: reporting requirements relating to AI-driven cyber incidents, AI-identified cyber vulnerabilities and cyber-related AI safety incidents (including obligations, thresholds, pathways and systems); Commonwealth governance and information-sharing arrangements for managing incidents involving AI (including roles, responsibilities and escalation pathways); engagement and information-sharing obligations of AI firms (including notification requirements and cooperation arrangements during incidents); the adequacy of existing system and legislative, regulatory and enforcement frameworks in deterring AI-driven cyber incidents (including whether current offences, liabilities, penalties and enforcement mechanisms are sufficient and effective); and mechanisms to strengthen networks and systems of government departments and agencies against AI vulnerabilities. PM&C states the review will also inform Australia's AI Standards and international work on safety incident reporting. The Prime Minister's disclosure of the underlying OpenAI / Medicare statistics portal incident is recorded separately as timeline event tl-2026-09-24-pm-discloses-openai-medicare-portal-access. This record is the government rapid review with published terms of reference; it is not a completed instrument and it is not OpenAI's later company taskforce.

title: New AI frontier cyber threat guidance for boards of directors

analysis.summary: Boards of directors and senior leaders need to understand how newer frontier AI models are reshaping cyber threats. As advances in frontier AI models make it easier for cybercriminals to identify and exploit vulnerabilities, organisations face a growing threat from AI-enabled cyber attacks. proposedRecord.title: Guidance Note: Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Commission Cases
proposedRecord.description: Fair Work Commission guidance note setting mandatory disclosure and verification requirements for generative AI used to prepare documents lodged in Commission cases, commencing 20 October 2026.
proposedRecord.content: Published on 24 August 2026 and commencing on 20 October 2026, following an exposure draft released for consultation on 24 March 2026. The guidance note applies whenever generative AI is used to create, write, edit, modify or otherwise prepare an application to the Commission or any other document to be lodged in a Commission case; using generative AI only to check spelling or grammar, or to format a document, is excluded. Three requirements apply. Requirement 1: the document must state that generative AI was used and how it was used. Requirement 2: the person must check the document and make any necessary changes so that all details are correct and relevant, and must state in the document that this was done — the checks cover whether references to facts and evidence are correct and the facts and evidence exist, whether cases, legislation, textbooks and articles cited exist and support the legal positions claimed, and whether extracts and quotes are accurate and come from the stated sources. The Commission states the checking must be done by a person and cannot be delegated to the same or a different generative AI tool. Requirement 3: where the document is a witness statement or declaration, the witness or declarant must check that it is based on their own knowledge, reflects their own words and is true to the best of their knowledge, and must state that in the document. Professional representatives — lawyers, paid agents, employed human resources advisers, and union or employer organisation officers — must additionally include hyperlinks to all case law referred to in a document prepared using generative AI, where hyperlinks are available. Personal information about other people involved in a case and confidential case information should not be given to public generative AI tools. Non-compliance may result in documents being given less weight or disregarded, costs orders against the non-complying party, or dismissal of the case. The guidance note records that knowingly giving false or misleading information to the Commission is an offence under section 137.1 of the Criminal Code and that giving false or misleading sworn evidence is an offence under section 678 of the Fair Work Act, each punishable by up to 12 months' imprisonment. The Commission states the guidance note will be amended from time to time and that users are responsible for keeping up to date with its requirements. From 20 October 2026 some Commission forms will include a question about generative AI use.

proposedRecord.content: On 31 August 2026 the Attorney-General announced the release of a consultation paper and draft legislation to modernise Australia's privacy laws (https://ministers.ag.gov.au/media-centre/modernising-australias-privacy-laws-digital-age-31-08-2026). The Attorney-General's Department consultation hub (https://consultations.ag.gov.au/rights-and-protections/privacy-reform/) lists the consultation as opened on 31 August 2026 and closed on 18 September 2026. It publishes the Exposure Draft Privacy Amendment (Personal Data Protection) Bill 2026 (https://consultations.ag.gov.au/rights-and-protections/privacy-reform/user_uploads/exposure-draft-bill-2026.pdf) and a Consultation Paper (https://consultations.ag.gov.au/rights-and-protections/privacy-reform/user_uploads/consultation_paper.pdf). The department says the reforms will bolster privacy protections and help tackle emerging risks from new technologies, including artificial intelligence and wearable devices such as smart glasses, and that the Bill remains subject to further consideration by government. The minister's release lists the key measures: a fair and reasonable test for collecting and using personal information; a right to erasure against large digital platforms; stronger standards for consent; and limits on trading in personal information without clear permission. It says AI-powered tools and devices, such as connected vehicles that continuously collect and process personal information, amplify privacy risks. The reforms build on the Privacy Act Review and the Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024 (register id federal-privacy-and-other-legislation-amendment-act-2024) and follow the Government Response to the Privacy Act Review Report (register id government-response-privacy-act-review-report). The Bill had not been introduced to Parliament when this record was staged.

proposedRecord.title: Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2026-28
proposedRecord.description: Australian Federal Police strategy for a human-led, responsible approach to adopting AI in policing from 2026 to 2028. It sets five strategic goals and four adoption pillars: People, Process, Technology and Partnerships.
proposedRecord.content:
The Australian Federal Police (AFP) publishes the Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2026-28 at https://www.afp.gov.au/news-centre/publications/artificial-intelligence-strategy-2026-28, with the PDF at https://www.afp.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-09/Artificial-Intelligence-Strategy.pdf. In her foreword, Commissioner Krissy Barrett APM says the strategy commits the AFP to a human-led, responsible and transparent approach to AI, that AI will support, not replace, the judgement of AFP members, and that accountability for decisions always rests with the AFP.

Vision: to establish the AFP as a collaborative leader that brings law enforcement and the broader AI community together in applied responsible use of AI.

Strategic goals: counter the criminal threat from AI, including deepfakes, synthetic media and disinformation; strengthen data-driven decision making; safeguard member wellbeing by reducing exposure to harmful material such as child abuse material; empower creativity and workforce engagement; and enhance productivity through services such as transcription, translation, summarisation, video analytics and entity recognition.

Adoption pillars: People (AI knowledge, culture and leadership; human-led decision-making; safeguarding member wellbeing), Process (responsible AI governance and policies; operational alignment), Technology (investment in technology; end-to-end data management) and Partnerships (partnership and collaboration; public trust and transparency).

The AFP says it has fully adopted the guiding principles of the ANZPAA Responsible and Ethical Artificial Intelligence Framework: transparency, explainability, accountability, human oversight, fairness, skills and knowledge, proportionality and justifiability, reliability, and privacy and security. The strategy also names Australia's AI Ethics Principles, the National Framework for the Assurance of AI in Government, the Policy for the Responsible Use of AI in Government and the Voluntary AI Safety Standard as informing its approach.

The risks it names are AI system failure; overuse, inappropriate or reckless use; legal, ethical and privacy risk; reputational and public trust risk; and bias and hallucination. It says the AFP will establish mechanisms to measure progress across all strategic pillars. The strategy gives no specific measures.

proposedRecord.content: The DTA media release of 30 October 2026 (https://www.dta.gov.au/media-releases/ai-reference-architecture-new-blueprint-help-government-agencies-design-ai-systems) announces the AI Reference Architecture (AIRA) and a companion guide. The resource is https://www.digital.gov.au/ai-reference-architecture. The introduction (https://www.digital.gov.au/ai-reference-architecture/introduction) says AIRA provides an architectural foundation for designing, implementing and governing AI across the Australian Government and supports the AI Plan for the Australian Public Service 2025 (https://www.digital.gov.au/policy/ai/australian-public-service-ai-plan-2025) and the Policy for the responsible use of AI in government (https://www.digital.gov.au/ai/ai-in-government-policy; register id policy-responsible-use-ai-government-v2). It covers a functional stack (experience, application and orchestration, intelligence and analytics, data and metadata, platform and infrastructure), communication, trustworthiness and assurance, and human agency, oversight and control. Appendix A covers key roles (https://www.digital.gov.au/ai-reference-architecture/appendix-a). Appendix B covers the relationship with other frameworks (https://www.digital.gov.au/ai-reference-architecture/appendix-b). The Companion Guide — Scenarios is https://www.digital.gov.au/ai-reference-architecture/companion-guide. The landing page offers https://www.digital.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/2026-10/AI-Architecture-ACCESSIBLE.pdf and https://www.digital.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/2026-10/AI-Architecture-Companion-Guide-ACCESSIBLE.pdf, each marked last updated 23 Oct 2026. The release says using the architecture is voluntary: it supports agencies to meet applicable requirements and does not replace them.

The resource is https://www.digital.gov.au/ai-reference-architecture. The introduction (https://www.digital.gov.au/ai-reference-architecture/introduction) says AIRA provides an architectural foundation for designing, implementing and governing AI across the Australian Government and supports the AI Plan for the Australian Public Service 2025 (https://www.digital.gov.au/policy/ai/australian-public-service-ai-plan-2025) and the Policy for the responsible use of AI in government (https://www.digital.gov.au/ai/ai-in-government-policy; register id policy-responsible-use-ai-government-v2). It covers a functional stack (experience, application and orchestration, intelligence and analytics, data and metadata, platform and infrastructure), communication, trustworthiness and assurance, and human agency, oversight and control. Appendix A covers key roles (https://www.digital.gov.au/ai-reference-architecture/appendix-a). Appendix B covers the relationship with other frameworks (https://www.digital.gov.au/ai-reference-architecture/appendix-b). The Companion Guide — Scenarios is https://www.digital.gov.au/ai-reference-architecture/companion-guide. The landing page offers https://www.digital.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/2026-10/AI-Architecture-ACCESSIBLE.pdf and https://www.digital.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/2026-10/AI-Architecture-Companion-Guide-ACCESSIBLE.pdf, each marked last updated 23 Oct 2026. The release says using the architecture is voluntary: it supports agencies to meet applicable requirements and does not replace them.

proposedRecord.title: NESA Stage 6 take-home assessment and generative AI rules
proposedRecord.description: ACE Rules cap take-home assessment in each Preliminary and HSC course at one task weighted no more than 15%, except in exempt courses, require marks to reflect students’ own work rather than generative-AI use, and require schools not to rely on software tools that detect generative AI when determining malpractice.

source.title: New limit on take-home assessment tasks from Term 4 2026

proposedRecord.content: NESA announced the changes on 31 August 2026 and has written them into the ACE Rules. The pages for Rule 2.1 (formal assessment programs and tasks) and Rule 10.1 (breaches and malpractice) show "Last updated: 15 September 2026" and change notices dated 16 September 2026. Under Rule 2.1, for each HSC course schools "must not exceed one take-home assessment task, worth a maximum of 15%", except for exempt courses with major projects or HSC practical exams, and the same limit applies to each Preliminary course, except for courses that are a prerequisite for an exempt HSC course. Schools must design formal tasks so marks reflect students’ own work and not their use of generative AI, and teachers must award marks based on evidence of the student’s own knowledge, skills and understanding, "and not the use of generative artificial intelligence". Rule 10.1 requires schools to "not rely on software tools for the detection of generative artificial intelligence" when determining whether malpractice has occurred. NESA’s notice says the limit starts from Term 4, 2026 for HSC courses and Term 1, 2027 for Preliminary courses. NESA had not stated exact day-level commencement dates when this record was reviewed.

proposedRecord.title: The Use of Generative AI — Guidelines for Judicial Officers
proposedRecord.description: Queensland Courts guidelines governing judicial officers' and their staff's use of generative AI, revised on 15 September 2025.
proposedRecord.content: First issued on 13 May 2024 and reissued in a revised version on 15 September 2025, these Guidelines govern the use of generative AI by Queensland judicial officers and their staff. They open with the principle that any use of generative AI tools by judicial officers and their staff must be consistent with the fulfilment of the judiciary's obligation to do equal justice to all persons according to law. They address what generative AI is and how it fails, the confidentiality of court information and the risks of entering it into publicly available tools, and the limits on relying on generative AI output in the exercise of the judicial function, including in the preparation of reasons. The revised version also addresses the intersection with expert evidence: it directs judicial officers to consider whether generative AI has been used in the formulation or expression of an opinion contained in an expert report, and whether the expert should be required to identify in their report the precise way in which they have used AI. That provision sits alongside Supreme Court of Queensland Practice Direction Number 14 of 2024 on expert evidence in criminal proceedings, which was amended and reissued on 10 September 2025 to add generative AI requirements for experts. The Guidelines are the bench-facing counterpart to the Queensland Courts guidelines for non-lawyers and to the Accuracy of References in Submissions practice directions issued across the Queensland hierarchy. A version history at the end of the document records both the original issue on 13 May 2024 and the revision on 15 September 2025.

proposedRecord.title: The Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) — Guidelines for Responsible Use by Non-Lawyers
proposedRecord.description: Queensland Courts plain-language guidelines for self-represented litigants and other non-lawyers using generative AI in civil and criminal proceedings.
proposedRecord.content: These Guidelines apply to civil and criminal proceedings in Queensland courts and tribunals, including the Supreme Court, District Court and Planning and Environment Court, and are directed to people who are not lawyers. They are the litigant-facing counterpart to the Queensland Courts guidelines for judicial officers and to the Accuracy of References in Submissions practice directions issued across the Queensland court and tribunal hierarchy; QCAT Practice Direction No 10 of 2025 directs self-represented litigants to read them and records that they were updated on 15 September 2025. The Guidelines explain in plain language what generative AI chatbots are and what they can usefully do, including summarising material, changing tone or format, generating new text or a plan for new text in a specific format, and answering questions on a topic. They emphasise that these tools can get information wrong, that AI-generated content should never be assumed to be correct, and that a person who puts material before a court remains responsible for its accuracy whether or not generative AI helped produce it. They address the risk of fabricated cases, citations and legislative references, the need to check anything a chatbot produces against an authoritative source before relying on it, and the privacy and confidentiality risks of entering personal or case information into publicly available tools. The document prints the date 15 September 2025 and a version history recording 'Guideline issued on 13 May 2024' and 'Revised version issued on 15 September 2025'; QCAT Practice Direction No 10 of 2025 likewise cites the Guidelines as 'updated 15 September 2025'.

proposedRecord.title: Litigants in Person Practice Note (GPN-LIP)
proposedRecord.description: Federal Court of Australia general practice note for litigants in person, issued by Chief Justice Mortimer on 5 March 2026, which at paragraphs 2.8 to 2.11 directs self-represented litigants on when they may and may not use generative AI programs.
proposedRecord.content: GPN-LIP is a General Practice Note of the Federal Court of Australia written in plain language for litigants in person, that is, parties who have a legal case in the Court without a lawyer. It is issued under the Federal Court of Australia Act 1976 (Cth) and litigants are asked to sign an acknowledgement form confirming they have read it. Its generative AI provisions sit in Part 2 (Getting legal help). Paragraph 2.8 directs litigants not to use generative AI programs such as ChatGPT, Claude, Microsoft Copilot or Google Gemini to obtain legal help about whether they have a case they can win, because such programs are not reliable, are not trained like lawyers, may give answers based on American law and can give false answers to legal questions. Paragraph 2.9 similarly warns against social media and pseudolaw sites, noting a litigant can be in serious trouble for making arguments not based on real law. Paragraph 2.10 permits litigants who start or defend a case based on real law and evidence to use AI programs to help explain their case to the Court, but requires them to tell the Court they have done so if asked, to check that all facts from AI programs are correct and complete and that the law is correct, preferably with a lawyer or otherwise using the free legal research databases listed in Attachment D, and warns of serious consequences for giving the Court false information about facts or law. Paragraph 2.11 states the Court will soon publish more about what litigants can and cannot do with AI programs in their cases; that further guidance was issued as GPN-AI on 16 April 2026. The remainder of the practice note covers interpreters, the Court's expectations of litigants in person, the registry, hearings and costs, and includes four attachments on definitions, sections 37M and 37N of the Act, other practice notes and legal research databases.
proposedRecord.aiSummary: The Federal Court's litigants in person practice note tells self-represented parties not to rely on generative AI to assess whether they have a winnable case, permits AI to help explain a case founded on real law and evidence, and requires them to disclose AI use on request and verify every fact and legal proposition.

proposedRecord.content: On 24 September 2026 the Prime Minister announced a Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet (PM&C)-led rapid review of whether existing legislative, governance and information-sharing arrangements are fit for purpose to prepare for and respond to cyber incidents involving artificial intelligence. PM&C published formal terms of reference the same day (https://www.pmc.gov.au/resources/terms-reference-rapid-review-australian-government-arrangements-ai-driven-cyber-incident; release date Thursday 24 September 2026). The review page states that PM&C leads the review in collaboration with the National Cyber Security Coordinator, the Australian Signals Directorate, the Australian AI Safety Institute and Services Australia. Per the terms of reference, recommendations scope covers: reporting requirements relating to AI-driven cyber incidents, AI-identified cyber vulnerabilities and cyber-related AI safety incidents (including obligations, thresholds, pathways and systems); Commonwealth governance and information-sharing arrangements for managing incidents involving AI (including roles, responsibilities and escalation pathways); engagement and information-sharing obligations of AI firms (including notification requirements and cooperation arrangements during incidents); the adequacy of existing system and legislative, regulatory and enforcement frameworks in deterring AI-driven cyber incidents (including whether current offences, liabilities, penalties and enforcement mechanisms are sufficient and effective); and mechanisms to strengthen networks and systems of government departments and agencies against AI vulnerabilities. PM&C states the review will also inform Australia's AI Standards and international work on safety incident reporting. The Prime Minister's disclosure of the underlying OpenAI / Medicare statistics portal incident is recorded separately as timeline event tl-2026-09-24-pm-discloses-openai-medicare-portal-access. This record is the government rapid review with published terms of reference; it is not a completed instrument and it is not OpenAI's later company taskforce.

proposedRecord.content: Schedule 1[81] inserts sections 189A and 189B into the Electoral Act 2017. Section 189A prohibits printing, publishing, distributing or publicly displaying, during the regulated period, digitally generated electoral material that depicts a simulated person performing an act the real person did not perform (maximum penalty for an individual 60 penalty units or 6 months imprisonment, or both; otherwise 300 penalty units). It is a defence that the real person gave written consent, or that the defendant took no part in the content and could not reasonably have known. Digitally generated electoral material means electoral material with audio visual, visual or audio content generated substantially, or modified or altered significantly, by artificial intelligence, excluding cartoons and animated drawings. Section 189B requires digitally generated electoral material depicting a digitally created person, event or place that a reasonable person would think is real to include a written or spoken statement that it is digitally generated electoral material (maximum penalty for an individual 20 penalty units or 6 months imprisonment, or both; otherwise 100 penalty units).
proposedRecord.aiSummary: NSW election law that bans deceptive AI-generated depictions of real people in electoral material during the regulated period and requires other AI-generated electoral material to be labelled. In force since 7 April 2026.

proposedRecord.content: The Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026 was introduced and read a first time in the House of Representatives on 15 October 2026, and the second reading was moved that day. Status is proposed: the register has no separate before-Parliament status. The bill is not an Act. The House progress page (https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/Bills_Search_Results/Result?bId=r7553) records that introduction, the second reading, portfolio Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts, and referral on 15 October 2026 to the Senate Environment and Communications Legislation Committee, with a report due on 20 November 2026. That reporting date is stored as scheduled_review because the register has no committee-report date type. It is the committee's reporting date, not a statutory review of an Act. As described in the approved 11–17 October 2026 signal, the bill covers services that generate material using AI (s 25B(1)(h)), requires yearly risk assessments, and in Schedule 3 would repeal the online-safety industry codes and standards 12 months after Royal Assent. Those codes remain in force on esafety-genai-industry-codes. An exposure draft was released for targeted consultation on 8 September 2026 (Minister for Communications, https://minister.infrastructure.gov.au/wells/media-release/my-feed-my-way). The Minister announced introduction on 15 October 2026 (https://minister.infrastructure.gov.au/wells/media-release/digital-duty-care-next-step-australias-world-leading-reforms). The department's page is https://www.infrastructure.gov.au/media-communications/internet/online-safety/digital-duty-care. Secondary reports, not the canonical source: https://www.openaustralia.org.au/debates/?id=2026-10-15.6.2 and https://aigeek.au/news/digital-duty-of-care-bill-introduced-ai/.
proposedRecord.aiSummary: Proposed Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026, introduced on 15 October 2026. It is not law. The Senate Environment and Communications Legislation Committee is due to report on 20 November 2026.

title: ASIC Market Integrity Rules amendments for AI-enabled and automated trading
notes: Re-verification of the hidden draft record with fresh evidence, for an editorial decision card.

analysis.summary: ASIC is strengthening safeguards for automated and AI-enabled trading while streamlining regulatory requirements for securities and futures market participants under incoming changes to its Market Integrity Rules (MIRs). The reforms bolster important gatekeeper controls requiring participants to test, monitor and govern trading systems and algorithms as markets evolve and the adoption of AI increases. These controls sit alongside market operators’ anomalous order thresholds and extreme trade ranges, providing an important safeguard for the integrity and resilience of Australian markets.

proposedRecord.description: ASIC amendments to the securities and futures Market Integrity Rules that modernise trading-system and automated-trading obligations, including for algorithmic and AI-enabled trading. ASIC made the ASIC Market Integrity Rules (Securities Markets) Amendment Instrument 2026/574 (F2026L01223) and the ASIC Market Integrity Rules (Futures Markets) Amendment Instrument 2026/575 (F2026L01224) on 15 September 2026; both were registered on 17 September 2026 and tabled in both Houses on 12 October 2026. Each commences 18 months after registration: the Federal Register schedules the securities amendments to start on 17 March 2028, while ASIC's CS 63 states 18 March 2028. Media release 26-226MR is dated 24 September 2026. Consultation CS 63 on updated RG 265 and RG 266 closes at 5 pm AEDT on 5 November 2026.

proposedRecord.content: ASIC media release 26-226MR (https://www.asic.gov.au/about-asic/news-centre/find-a-media-release/2026-releases/26-226mr-asic-strengthens-ai-trading-safeguards-and-streamlines-market-integrity-rules) is dated 24 September 2026 on the page (displayDate). It announces amendments to the ASIC Market Integrity Rules (Securities Markets) 2017 and the ASIC Market Integrity Rules (Futures Markets) 2017 that modernise trading-systems obligations for algorithmic trading, including AI and machine learning, require participants to test, monitor and govern trading systems and algorithms, align more closely with IOSCO principles, apply trading-system requirements consistently to manually entered and automated orders, and clarify the false or misleading appearance rule for AI-enabled and other trading. The release says the amendments follow Consultation Paper 386 and take effect in 2028 after an 18-month transition. The release does not mention a kill switch or a seven-year record-keeping period. ASIC consultation CS 63 (https://www.asic.gov.au/regulatory-resources/find-a-document/consultations/cs-63-proposed-updates-to-rg-265-and-rg-266-and-withdrawal-of-rg-241) states Released 24 September 2026 and that comments close at 5 pm AEDT on 5 November 2026. It states that the market integrity rules were amended in September 2026 and that the rules commence on 18 March 2028 after an 18-month transition. It proposes updates to RG 265 and RG 266 and moving relevant guidance from RG 241 into those guides so RG 241 can be retired. The CS 63 page does not mention a kill switch or seven-year record keeping. Attachments 5 and 6, the marked-up compilations of the securities and futures rules, state that the changes are in force from 18 March 2028 and that market participants and market operators can continue to comply with the rules as in force on 15 October 2024 until 18 March 2028. The Federal Register of Legislation records ASIC Market Integrity Rules (Securities Markets) Amendment Instrument 2026/574 (F2026L01223, https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2026L01223/latest/text) and ASIC Market Integrity Rules (Futures Markets) Amendment Instrument 2026/575 (F2026L01224, https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2026L01224/latest/text). Each instrument is dated 15 September 2026 and was registered on 17 September 2026. Section 2 of each instrument states that it commences on the day that is 18 months after the day it is registered. The instruments do not use the term kill switch. They do set seven-year record obligations in the amended trading-system rules. It proposes updates to RG 265 and RG 266 and moving relevant guidance from RG 241 into those guides so RG 241 can be retired. The CS 63 page does not mention a kill switch or seven-year record keeping. Attachments 5 and 6, the marked-up compilations of the securities and futures rules, state that the changes are in force from 18 March 2028 and that market participants and market operators can continue to comply with the rules as in force on 15 October 2024 until 18 March 2028. analysis.summary: Determination made by the Minister for Communications under section 45 of the Online Safety Act 2021 setting out the Australian Government's basic online safety expectations for social media, relevant electronic and designated internet services. The Online Safety (Basic Online Safety Expectations) Amendment Determination 2024 added section 8A, which expects providers whose services use or enable generative AI capabilities to take reasonable steps to build in safety measures and to minimise the use of those capabilities to produce unlawful or harmful material, and section 8B on recommender systems. The amendment took effect on 31 May 2024.

proposedRecord.content: The expectations are not directly enforceable, but the eSafety Commissioner can require providers to report on how they meet them and publish statements about compliance. Section 8A, inserted in 2024, gives examples of reasonable steps for generative AI capabilities: safety risk assessments across design, deployment and post-deployment, explanatory tools for end users, keeping unlawful or harmful material out of training data, and detecting and preventing prompts that generate unlawful or harmful material.

agencies: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner
proposedRecord.content: Schedule 1 amends the Privacy Act 1988, including a Children's Online Privacy Code, new enforcement and declaration powers for the Information Commissioner, and Part 15 "Automated decisions and privacy policies". Part 15 inserts Australian Privacy Principles 1.7 to 1.9: where an APP entity has arranged for a computer program to make, or do a thing substantially and directly related to making, a decision that could reasonably be expected to significantly affect an individual's rights or interests, and personal information is used in the program, its APP privacy policy must say what kinds of personal information are used and what kinds of decisions are made. Schedule 2 inserts a statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy. Schedule 3 amends the Criminal Code to create offences for doxxing.
proposedRecord.aiSummary: Federal privacy reforms assented on 10 December 2024. New APP 1.7 to 1.9 require privacy policies to disclose automated decisions that significantly affect individuals, from 10 December 2026.

proposedRecord.content: The Act repeals and replaces section 474.17A of the Criminal Code. New subsection 474.17A(1) makes it an offence to use a carriage service to transmit material depicting, or appearing to depict, an adult engaged in a sexual pose or sexual activity where the person knows the depicted person does not consent or is reckless as to consent. A note says the offence covers images, videos or audio edited or entirely created using digital technology, including artificial intelligence ("deepfakes"). New section 474.17AA creates aggravated offences: one where 3 or more civil penalty orders under the Online Safety Act 2021 were made against the person beforehand, and one where the person also created or altered the material. Section 474.17B provides alternative verdicts.
proposedRecord.aiSummary: Commonwealth offences for sharing non-consensual sexual deepfakes of adults over a carriage service, with an aggravated offence for the person who created or altered the material. In force since 3 September 2024.

proposedRecord.content: The Act repeals and replaces section 474.17A of the Criminal Code. New subsection 474.17A(1) makes it an offence to use a carriage service to transmit material depicting, or appearing to depict, an adult engaged in a sexual pose or sexual activity where the person knows the depicted person does not consent or is reckless as to consent. A note says the offence covers images, videos or audio edited or entirely created using digital technology, including artificial intelligence ("deepfakes"). New section 474.17AA creates aggravated offences: one where 3 or more civil penalty orders under the Online Safety Act 2021 were made against the person beforehand, and one where the person also created or altered the material. Section 474.17B provides alternative verdicts.

proposedRecord.content: ASD's ACSC alert published on 25 September 2026. It reports instances of AI misalignment in which "AI agents have undertaken unexpected actions that were not intended or authorised by its operators": an agent given a task was limited by security controls on an organisation's public-facing website or service, then independently identified vulnerabilities and attempted to progress actions without direct human authorisation. ASD says there is no indication of a broader threat or malicious targeting against Australia, but that the case shows the importance of secure AI deployment and strong cyber security fundamentals. It is relevant to all Australian organisations with public-facing websites or applications. Mitigations are strong authentication, access controls and network segmentation; prompt identification and remediation of vulnerabilities; monitoring for unusual activity and regular log review; patching as soon as practicable; and testing controls and incident response procedures against AI-enabled threat scenarios. It asks organisations to report suspicious AI-driven activity to ASD and points to earlier ASD advice, including the blog 'When AI agents take unexpected actions'. It relates to ASD's agentic AI guidance (asd-careful-adoption-agentic-ai-services-2026, asd-agentic-ai-harnesses-2026).

proposedRecord.content: ASD advisory published on 29 September 2026. It says malicious cyber actors are obtaining unauthorised access to organisations' AI services through compromised API keys, stolen authentication tokens, compromised user sessions, vulnerable applications and third-party access arrangements, and that this access can be used to create harmful material, distill model capabilities, exhaust credits and disrupt legitimate work. It advises organisations to "treat access to advanced AI services as a security-sensitive asset" and not rely only on the AI developer's controls. Recommended actions are to keep an inventory of AI accounts, service identities and credentials with an accountable owner and least-privilege access; require phishing-resistant MFA, use managed devices and store API keys in approved secrets-management services; keep restricted-model access and sensitive data separate from routine and experimental use and give suppliers limited, auditable access; monitor model access, credential and permission changes, protect audit logs and configure tested spending, rate and consumption limits that enforce restrictions; and, on suspected compromise, revoke keys, sessions and tokens, preserve logs and fix the cause before restoring access. It notes that a compromised agent or session may reach connected enterprise systems, tools and data, and cites recent public reports of stolen AI API keys and unauthorised model access. Its audience tags are individuals and families, large organisations and critical infrastructure, and government. It complements ASD's agentic AI guidance (asd-careful-adoption-agentic-ai-services-2026, asd-agentic-ai-harnesses-2026).
proposedRecord.aiSummary: ASD advisory on securing AI service access: inventory and least privilege, phishing-resistant MFA, secrets management, usage monitoring with enforced spending limits, and incident response for compromised AI credentials.

proposedRecord.content: ASD published guidance on 9 April 2026 about the cyber security implications of increasingly capable frontier AI models, following Anthropic's 7 April 2026 announcement of Claude Mythos Preview. APRA's 30 April 2026 AI industry letter points regulated entities to ASD advice on frontier AI models.

proposedRecord.title: OAIC guidance on APP 1.7–1.9 transparency for automated decision-making
proposedRecord.description: OAIC guidance published 30 September 2026 on the Australian Privacy Principle 1.7–1.9 transparency obligation: from 10 December 2026 an APP entity must describe in its privacy policy the computer programs it has arranged to make, or to do something substantially and directly related to making, decisions that could reasonably be expected to significantly affect an individual's rights or interests.
agencies: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner
proposedRecord.content: The transparency obligation was inserted into Australian Privacy Principle 1 by the Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024 (Cth) and applies from 10 December 2026. APP 1.7 brings an APP entity into scope where it has arranged for a computer program to make a decision, or to do a thing substantially and directly related to making one; where that decision could reasonably be expected to significantly affect an individual's rights or interests; and where personal information about the individual is used in the program's operation. APP 1.8 then sets out what the entity's privacy policy must say: the kinds of personal information used in those programs, the kinds of decisions made solely by them, and the kinds of decisions for which the program does a thing substantially and directly related to the decision. The OAIC treats 'computer program' broadly, covering rule-based automation, machine learning, ordinary software and generative AI tools, and notes that human review of an output does not by itself take a decision out of scope. On 30 September 2026 the OAIC published three compliance resources — the APP 1.7-1.9 Transparency Obligation Fact Sheet (the record's cited source), a supplementary fact sheet for government agencies, and a flowchart — together with an update to its APP 1 Guidelines, after 90 written submissions to its earlier consultation. The register separately tracks the OAIC's 18 May 2026 consultation on automated decision-making transparency, which these resources answer, and its earlier guidance of 21 October 2024 on privacy and developing and training generative AI models and on privacy and the use of commercially available AI products.

proposedRecord.content: Published by ASD on 11 September 2026 and announced in the ASD news item 'ASD releases new guidance on the agentic AI harnesses' (https://www.cyber.gov.au/news/asd-releases-new-guidance-on-the-agentic-ai-harnesses). The publication treats the harness, rather than the model, as the part of an agentic AI system an organisation can most directly govern and secure. It describes the harness components (user interface, prompt and policy layer, context manager, model interface, tool registry, permission system, execution environment, connector layer, memory and session store, audit and observability, and the update and supply-chain path) and explains that prompt injection cannot be reliably fixed in the model, so controls must be enforced in the harness. Recommended controls include least-privilege access and a hardened, organisation-controlled execution environment; human approval for sensitive or high-impact actions; validation of tool parameters, outputs and agent work before operational use; logging of prompts, responses, tool invocations, approvals and configuration changes; cost monitoring to detect misuse or runaway agents; careful model selection; focused context and bounded sub-agents; and a persistent organisational rules file. It closes with governance questions for executives and advises a phased adoption that starts with low-risk use cases. It is written for executive decision-makers, CISOs and IT leaders, and complements ASD's 'Careful adoption of agentic AI services' guidance.
proposedRecord.aiSummary: ASD guidance on securing and governing the agentic AI harness: least privilege, human approval of high-impact actions, audit logging, monitoring and executive governance questions.

proposedRecord.content: The WA Government Artificial Intelligence Policy and Assurance Framework was first published on 5 March 2024 by the Office of Digital Government. proposedRecord.content: The Summary Offences (Humiliating, Degrading or Invasive Depictions) Amendment Act 2025 inserts Part 5B, sections 26F to 26J, into the Summary Offences Act 1953. It covers audiovisual, audio, or visual content generated wholly by artificial intelligence or created solely using digital technology that depicts a simulated real person. The Act creates offences for creating, distributing, or threatening to distribute humiliating, degrading, or invasive depictions, with consent-based and specified law-enforcement, legal-proceeding, and artistic-merit exceptions. Penalties vary by conduct and whether a purported real person is under 17, reaching $20,000 or four years imprisonment for creating or distributing an invasive depiction of a simulated person purporting to be a child. The Act was assented to on 22 May 2025 and commenced on 3 November 2025 under the official proclamation.

proposedRecord.content: Section 32 of the Electoral (Miscellaneous) Amendment Act 2024 inserts sections 115B to 115D into the Electoral Act 1985. The provisions prohibit distribution of an AI-generated electoral advertisement depicting a simulated real person performing an act they did not perform, subject to stated defences. They require prescribed AI-generated electoral advertisements to carry clear spoken or displayed disclosure statements, and empower the Electoral Commissioner to request withdrawal or a corrective statement and the Supreme Court to make corresponding orders. Maximum penalties for the principal prohibition and disclosure offences are $5,000 for a natural person and $10,000 for a body corporate. The Act was assented to on 5 December 2024; Part 2, including section 32, commenced on 10 October 2025 under the official commencement proclamation.

proposedRecord.content: From Monday 12 September 2020, OVIC's website will no longer be supported in Internet Explorer (IE). We recommend installing Microsoft Edge, Google Chrome, Safari, Firefox, or Opera to visit the site. Use of enterprise Generative AI tools in the Victorian public sector Last updated 26 June 2026 This guidance outlines the Office of the Victorian Information Commissioner’s (OVIC) minimum expectations for Victorian public sector organisations (VPS organisations) using enterprise Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) tools.1 It also sets out the key information privacy and information security obligations for VPS organisations to consider. Generative AI is a type of Artificial Intelligence that creates content, such as text, images, music, audio and video. Generative AI tools do this by predicting the best response to the information entered, known as a prompt. Predictions, also known as outputs, are made based on the content of the prompt and the data on which the Generative AI tool has been trained.2 This guidance relates to Generative AI tools that are purchased at an enterprise level, and operate within a VPS organisation’s securely managed environment. Enterprise Generative AI tools are integrated within an organisation’s existing systems. Examples include tenanted versions of Microsoft 365 Copilot, Chat GPT Enterprise, Duet AI for Google Workspace, Zoom IQ and Slack GPT. 3 The adoption and use of Generative AI tools may magnify existing information privacy and information security risks for VPS organisations, and create new ones (some examples are included below). VPS organisations should therefore take the steps outlined below to improve their information security maturity and privacy practices before adopting an enterprise Generative AI tool.4 The risks involved in using publicly available Generative AI tools are different to those involved in using enterprise Generative AI tools. For guidance on using publicly available Generative AI tools, please refer to OVIC’s guidance on the use of personal information with publicly available Generative AI tools in the Victorian public sector. OVIC’s minimum expectations This section sets out OVIC’s minimum expectations for VPS organisations to work through prior to purchasing and integrating an enterprise Generative AI tool. VPS organisations should: Assess the maturity of their existing information security program,5 including: identifying existing information holdings and systems that may be impacted by the introduction of an integrated Generative AI tool, including due consideration of their security value considering how any Generative AI outputs will be assessed, valued and securely managed, including applying appropriate protective markings for newly generated information assets conducting a security risk assessment for the integration of an enterprise Generative AI tool, including due consideration of adjusted risk profiles and development of treatment plans to address relevant Generative AI features implementing any updated treatment plans by rolling out new or changed controls, including consideration of the organisation’s existing logical access controls implementing a formal process for the ongoing monitoring and review of risks and controls. This is especially important given the dynamic development and release of enhancements and new features in Generative AI tools. Undertake privacy impact assessments (PIAs) to understand the ways in which the enterprise Generative AI tool will be utilised, the risks it presents to the privacy of individuals, whether and how those risks can be mitigated, and in light of any residual risks, the extent to which it is appropriate to proceed to purchase the tool.6 There may be high-risk functions or specific business units within a VPS organisation for whom it is not appropriate to use a Generative AI tool.7 Ensure that risks and controls are regularly reviewed and monitored. Be careful when using Generative AI tools in ways that may significantly impact one or more individuals. This includes automated decision-making and the use of these tools during earlier steps in a decision-making process, where that earlier use significantly influences or materially assists the organisation in making its decision. Earlier steps may include using a Generative AI tool to conduct research, summarise key information, facts or evidence or make a prediction, recommendation, assessment, summary, conclusion or inference. Using Generative AI tools in decision-making processes carries privacy risks under Victoria’s Information Privacy Principles (IPPs). This includes IPP 2 risks (where personal information is used for a secondary purpose that is not permitted), IPP 3 risks (poor data quality and accuracy) and IPP 1 risks (the collection of personal information may not be considered fair if collected for use in fully automated decision-making that significantly impacts on the individual). Ensure that settings can be configured to enhance information privacy and information security, such as disabling or limiting data sharing between certain platforms and between the VPS organisation and the company that owns the enterprise Generative AI tool. Develop organisational policies on the use of Generative AI tools, and communicate about the policies to staff, contracted service providers and other personnel. Develop and implement clear and tailored guidance and training for their staff, contracted service providers and other personnel on the use of the enterprise Generative AI tool, that: covers how to safely and responsibly use the enterprise Generative AI tool, prompt engineering, risk assessment and management, human review of generated outputs, and active monitoring and reviews to identify potential misuse ensures all users of the enterprise Generative AI tool are aware of and understand what information they are permitted to enter into the enterprise Generative AI tool and its permitted use cases ensures all users of the enterprise Generative AI tool are aware of how the tool may generate, collect, use or disclose personal information and public sector information, and understand how to ensure the accuracy and security of the information. Develop an incident response plan for dealing with inadvertent or unauthorised disclosures, access or misuse of information through the enterprise Generative AI tool. VPS organisations are responsible for all actions and content generated by the enterprise Generative AI tool they use. Where an information security incident or interference with privacy occurs through the use of the tool, VPS organisations will not be able to simply say that the incident or interference was caused by AI. Notify OVIC of information privacy and information security incidents, in line with the Information Security Incident Notification Scheme.8 Information privacy requirements This section applies to VPS organisations covered by Part 3 of the Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014 (PDP Act). The 10 Information Privacy Principles (IPPs), as set out in Schedule 1 of the PDP Act, will apply to the collection and handling of personal information that may be entered into, generated, or used by an enterprise Generative AI tool.9 While all 10 IPPs are relevant to the handling of personal information by an organisation, IPPs 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 will be most relevant when integrating an enterprise Generative AI tool.10 Collection of personal information IPP 1 sets out that an organisation must only collect personal information if it is necessary to fulfill one or more of its functions. The collection must be lawful, fair and not unreasonably intrusive. Organisations must also provide notice to individuals about why the information is being collected, how it will be used and how individuals can access the information. Organisations should understand that when an enterprise Generative AI tool generates new content in response to a user prompt (such as “draft me a summary of the main points in the document called ‘John Smith’s CV’”), this generated content constitutes a new collection of personal information. Organisations must comply with the requirements of IPP 1. Example – Collection of personal information via a collaboration platform An organisation’s HR team invites a Senior Operations Manager to a meeting via a collaboration platform to provide an update on an internal conduct investigation involving one of the manager’s staff. The manager realises at the last minute that they cannot attend, so asks the enterprise Generative AI tool within the collaboration platform to ‘follow’ the meeting so they can receive a recap of what was discussed. The HR team joins the meeting and see a message from the manager that they can no longer attend. They decide that without the manager, there is no point discussing the matter but, since they have all set aside 30 minutes for the meeting, they use the time to instead discuss another matter, relating to a different staff member’s request for family violence leave. The next day, the manager sends a prompt to the enterprise Generative AI tool within the collaboration platform, asking “what were the main points discussed at the meeting?”. The enterprise Generative AI tool responds with a summary of the details about the other staff member and their request for family violence leave. The generation of the summary content by the enterprise Generative AI tool is a collection of personal information, which would likely contravene at least IPP 1.1 (as the manager had no need to know that information). Use and disclosure of personal information IPP 2 provides that personal information may only be used or disclosed for the primary purpose for which it is was collected, or where an exception applies under IPPs 2.1(a-h). Human error is the leading cause of data breaches reported to OVIC involving unauthorised use and disclosure of personal information. Without proper controls in place, the implementation of an enterprise Generative AI tool could exacerbate this, given the increased speed at which personal information can be generated, used, and disclosed. While users are in control of what they do with content generated by an enterprise Generative AI tool, there is a risk that humans using a tool described as ‘intelligent’ may not always exercise an appropriate level of scrutiny over its output. Further, as enterprise Generative AI tools use documents from an organisation’s information holdings to generate content in response to a user prompt, they could provide the user with personal information with which they were previously unfamiliar (even if access controls are correctly configured and the user has a right to know this information). This creates a risk that VPS employees could be unaware of the original purpose for which the personal information was collected, and cannot properly consider whether a proposed use or disclosure would comply with IPP 2. Example – Unauthorised disclosure of personal information generated by an enterprise Generative AI tool An organisation’s Assessment Officer wants to write a letter rejecting Person A’s application for a service. They prompt their enterprise Generative AI tool to draft this letter and base it off a letter they wrote two months ago rejecting Person B’s application. Impressed by how quickly the enterprise Generative AI tool drafts the six-page letter, the Assessment Officer quickly reads through and digitally signs it. They then send the letter to Person A by email. Person A later calls the Complaints Officer and informs them that while the letter was addressed to Person A, it also contained the name of Person B in the body of the letter as well as other personal information relating to Person B’s application. As well as highlighting an interference with Person B’s privacy, Person A also suspects that the Assessment Officer may have based their decision on the wrong personal information, and asks that their application is considered afresh. The disclosure of Person B’s personal information to Person A is a breach of IPP 2. The use of inaccurate personal information about Person A would also likely breach IPP 3, relating to accuracy of personal information (see discussion below). Additionally, this scenario raises concerns about the fairness of the decision made. Accuracy of personal information IPP 3 requires an organisation to take reasonable steps to ensure the personal information it collects, uses or discloses is accurate, complete and up to date. The use of an enterprise Generative AI tool presents an increased risk of organisations generating, using or disclosing inaccurate personal information. This is because Generative AI outputs will not always give the correct information. They simply make predictions based on the prompt they receive and the training they’ve had. Further, where a user re-generates the same prompt, the Generative AI tool likely won’t reproduce the original output. In choosing whether to implement an enterprise Generative AI tool, organisations should assess whether they will be able to mitigate risks associated with the generation of inaccurate, incomplete or outdated personal information. Example – Summary of complaint documents present incomplete picture A complainant makes a complaint to a regulator about the actions of a government department. In a 20-page document, the complainant sets out comprehensive details of their allegations, the serious harm they have experienced, and what they want the department to do to resolve their concerns, including payment of $20,000 in compensation. The complaint is assigned to a Complaint Officer at the regulator’s office. After reading the complaint once, the Officer writes a prompt to an enterprise Generative AI tool asking it to summarise the content into a new document, and directs that it should be two pages long. Once generated, the Officer emails the summary to the department asking for its response to the complaint. The department responds, agreeing that the conduct occurred as alleged but insists that it was a trivial matter that had little impact on the complainant. The department offers $1,000 in compensation to resolve the complaint. The complainant rejects this, and the regulator closes the complaint on the basis that it cannot be resolved. The complainant is disappointed by the department’s approach and asks the Complaint Officer how a government body could read her complaint and still place so little value on what she went through. The Officer explains that it was actually an AI-generated summary of the complaint that was sent to the department, and provides the complainant with a copy. The complainant is shocked when they read the summary. They believe it has omitted crucial elements of their allegations, and has minimised their description of the harm suffered. They believe it has created an inaccurate and incomplete description of the complaint, and has led to the department trivialising their experience and dismissing the complaint. The collection and use of inaccurate personal information about the complainant would likely breach IPP 3, as the regulator has not taken reasonable steps to make sure that the personal information it collects, uses or discloses is accurate and complete. Security of personal information IPP 4 requires an organisation to take reasonable steps to protect the personal information it holds from misuse, loss, and unauthorised access, modification and disclosure. The adoption of an enterprise Generative AI tool could magnify existing risks to the security of personal information for organisations. One particular risk relates to unauthorised access to information, where access permissions have not been properly configured within other organisational systems that are then integrated with the enterprise Generative AI tool. Misconfiguration of access controls is one of the most common causes of data breaches reported to OVIC.11 Organisations should review and update access controls for any platforms integrated with enterprise Generative AI tools. Further information on steps organisations should take in relation to security controls is covered in the next section. Example – Unauthorised access due to misconfigured access controls A manager is drafting an internal document for a new member of their team to explain the basics of performance development procedures. Looking for inspiration, the manager prompts an enterprise Generative AI tool, asking about any previous documents relating to performance development that other staff in the organisation have created. Due to an access control misconfiguration, of which the manager was unaware, the Generative AI tool sends the manager a range of documents that include final copies of the Performance Development Plans of their colleagues. The disclosure of the Performance Development Plans of other colleagues to the manager due to misconfigured access controls would likely be a breach of IPP 4.1. Privacy policies IPP 5 requires VPS organisations to have a privacy policy, outlining how they handle the personal information they hold. Where personal information is handled by an enterprise Generative AI tool, a VPS organisation’s privacy policy should be clear about this. This is especially important where the outputs of an enterprise Generative AI tool are used to inform decision making about an individual, such as whether they are eligible for a service or a payment. Information security requirements Before VPS organisations implement any enterprise Generative AI tool, the public sector body head must assess the information security risks to the confidentiality, integrity and availability of public sector information and systems proposed to be used by the enterprise Generative AI tool,12 and ensure adherence to the Victorian Protective Data Security Standards (the Standards).13 The Standards set out the mandatory requirements to protect public sector information across all security domains including governance, information, personnel, information communications technology and physical security. The PDP Act extends these information security obligations to contracted service providers (CSPs), requiring public sector body heads to ensure that a CSP does not do an act or engage in a practice that contravenes a Standard.14 VPS organisations therefore must ensure their security risk assessment includes an evaluation of CSPs relevant to the enterprise Generative AI tool. By following this approach organisations: will be best placed to understand the risks of an enterprise Generative AI tool within the context of their organisation and risk profile will ensure that any changes to their operating environment (people, processes and technology) are incorporated into existing risk assessments provide the public sector body head with full visibility and understanding of current risks associated with an enterprise Generative AI tool following any changes. For the purpose of this guidance, VPS organisations are organisations subject to Parts 3 and 4 of the Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014. See sections 3 and 84 of that Act for a list of organisations covered by these Parts.For further information on Generative AI concepts, see the resource developed by the Centre of Excellence for Automated Decision-Making and Society, and OVIC: https://www.admscentre.org.au/genai-concepts/This guidance replaces the guidance OVIC issued in its public statement on the use of Microsoft 365 Copilot in the Victorian public sector in October 2023.OVIC recommends that VPS organisations review OVIC’s guidance on engaging third party providers prior to purchasing an enterprise Generative AI tool. The guidance outlines the steps VPS organisations should take to ensure they meet their information privacy and information security obligations: https://ovic.vic.gov.au/privacy/resources-for-organisations/engaging-contracted-service-providers/See the information security requirements section below.OVIC has a PIA template and accompanying guide available to assist organisations to undertake a PIA: https://ovic.vic.gov.au/privacy/resources-for-organisations/privacy-impact-assessment/It likely will not be sufficient for one overarching PIA to be undertaken on the integration of the enterprise Generative AI tool. PIAs should be conducted for individual functions or uses of the enterprise Generative AI tool, or by business unit, where a business unit will use the Generative AI tool for a discrete, defined purpose.Incidents can be reported via OVIC’s incident notification form: https://ovic.vic.gov.au/privacy/resources-for-organisations/information-security-and-privacy-incident-notification-form/Personal information is defined in section 3 of the Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014 as ‘information or an opinion… that is recorded in any form and whether true or not, about an individual whose identity is apparent, or can reasonably be ascertained, from the information or opinion’. The definition of personal information excludes health information, which is covered by the Health Records Act 2001.For guidance on how to interpret and apply the IPPs, refer to OVIC’s Guidelines to the Information Privacy Principles: https://ovic.vic.gov.au/privacy/resources-for-organisations/guidelines-to-the-information-privacy-principles/OVIC Incidents Insights Report: 1 July 2022 – 31 December 2022: https://ovic.vic.gov.au/information-security/security-insights/incident-insights-report-1-july-2022-31-december-2022/Public sector data, also known as public sector information, is defined in section 3 of the PDP Act as ‘information (including personal information) obtained, received or held by an agency or body to which Part 4 applies’.The Victorian Protective Data Security Standards are available at: https://ovic.vic.gov.au/information-security/standards/Section 88(2), PDP Act.
