proposedRecord.description: Commonwealth policy setting mandatory requirements for the safe, transparent, and accountable use of AI by non-corporate Commonwealth entities.
proposedRecord.content: Version 2.1 is the live text. This version of the policy came into effect 15 December 2025 (v2.0), with minor updates published on 21 October 2026 (v2.1). It applies to all non-corporate Commonwealth entities, with specified exceptions. It requires accountable officials, transparency statements, a strategic approach to AI adoption, operational controls for responsible AI use, AI use-case accountability and registers, staff training, and AI use-case impact assessments. Appendix D (https://www.digital.gov.au/ai/ai-in-government-policy/policy-responsible-use-ai-government-version-21-appendix-d-classification-system-ai-use) classifies AI use into seven usage patterns: decision-making and administrative action, analytics, strategic support, workplace productivity, workflow automation, image processing, and coding. Decision-making and administrative action: Uses AI to make, or substantially and directly inform, a decision or administrative action that could affect the rights or interests of an individual or entity. This includes refusing or failing to take such an action. Standard for AI transparency statements 2.1: https://www.digital.gov.au/ai/ai-in-government-policy/standard-ai-transparency-statements (https://www.digital.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/2026-10/Standard%20for%20AI%20transparency%20statements%202_1.pdf). analysis.summary: Determination made by the Minister for Communications under section 45 of the Online Safety Act 2021 setting out the Australian Government's basic online safety expectations for social media, relevant electronic and designated internet services. proposedRecord.content: Circular to Practitioners No. 14 of 2026, dated 21 October 2026 and signed by Registrar Penelope Ikedife, publishes Guidelines for the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence. The circular says the guidelines apply to all court users, including lawyers, litigants, witnesses and other third parties who produce documents to the Court, in all Supreme Court proceedings, and that they commence that day until further notice. The guidelines (as at 21 October 2026) say they apply when court users use generative AI to help create, write, edit, modify or otherwise prepare a document for court proceedings (para 2.1). Part 3 calls for caution with pleadings, written submissions, lists of documents and other documents (paras 3.2 to 3.4), and particular caution with affidavit materials, witness statements and other witness evidence (para 3.5). Expert reports must contain the expert’s own opinion and process of reasoning and comply with the relevant practice direction and Expert Witness Code of Conduct (para 3.6). Court users should not enter confidential, privileged or private information, including information subject to a suppression or non-publication order, into an AI tool that is not a closed tool (para 3.8). Any person who uses generative AI to prepare a document must verify all content before submitting it, and AI-generated content must be checked by a person, not solely by a generative AI tool (paras 4.1 and 4.3). Court users are not required to certify the use of generative AI, but must disclose that use if asked, and a person who uses it is expected to be able to explain the tool, how it was used, and the checks (paras 4.4 and 4.5). Inconsistent use may lead to less weight, a document being disregarded, adjournment, costs, or dismissal, and for lawyers a referral to the Legal Profession Board of Tasmania or personal costs orders (paras 5.1 and 5.2).
proposedRecord.aiSummary: Supreme Court of Tasmania guidelines, commencing 21 October 2026, for all court users in all proceedings: verify generative AI documents, take particular care with pleadings and evidence, keep confidential material out of open tools, and disclose use if asked.

proposedRecord.content: The Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026 was introduced and read a first time in the House of Representatives on 15 October 2026, and the second reading was moved that day. On 28 October 2026 the bill home page records that the second reading was agreed, that consideration in detail agreed 15 government amendments and 8 crossbench amendments, and that the third reading was agreed. Status remains proposed: the register has no separate before-Parliament status, and the bill is not an Act. The same page's Status field still reads "Before Reps" and it shows no Senate progress table. The page records referral on 15 October 2026 to the Senate Environment and Communications Legislation Committee, with a report due on 20 November 2026. That reporting date is stored as scheduled_review because the register has no committee-report date type. It is the committee's reporting date, not a statutory review of an Act. Divisions listed on the bill home page for 28 October 2026 include the question that the amendments moved by Ms Chaney be agreed to. The sheet linked from that page (Kate Chaney MP, https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22legislation/amend/r7553_amend_94de72af-fd1a-4779-b6c7-c0230408dc0f%22) proposes inserting paragraph 25E(1)(da), "material or conduct that simulates emotional intimacy and encourages or fosters a child's dependence on it in place of human relationships". The third-reading PDF was not readable in this capture, so that sentence is the circulated sheet, not a quotation from the text as agreed. As described in the approved 11–17 October 2026 signal, the bill covers services that generate material using AI (s 25B(1)(h)), requires yearly risk assessments, and in Schedule 3 would repeal the online-safety industry codes and standards 12 months after Royal Assent. Those codes remain in force on esafety-genai-industry-codes. An exposure draft was released for targeted consultation on 8 September 2026 (Minister for Communications, https://minister.infrastructure.gov.au/wells/media-release/my-feed-my-way). The Minister announced introduction on 15 October 2026 (https://minister.infrastructure.gov.au/wells/media-release/digital-duty-care-next-step-australias-world-leading-reforms). The department's page is https://www.infrastructure.gov.au/media-communications/internet/online-safety/digital-duty-care.

proposedRecord.description: Western Australia’s whole-of-government AI policy and assurance framework, first published 5 March 2024 and with the current policy document updated June 2025, requiring AI Accountable Officers and lifecycle self-assessment of AI and automated-decision-making projects.
agencies: Department of the Premier and Cabinet
proposedRecord.content: The WA Government Artificial Intelligence Policy and Assurance Framework was first published on 5 March 2024 by the Office of Digital Government. The current policy document states that it was updated in June 2025. Government entities must nominate an AI Accountable Officer and use the AI Assurance Framework self-assessment for any system or project driven by AI or automated decision making, applying it throughout the project lifecycle. The project lead submits the assessment for approval by the entity’s AI Accountable Officer. Assessments must also be submitted to the WA Government AI Advisory Board when residual risk is mid-range or higher, Digital Capability Fund funding applies, or total project cost exceeds $5 million. The Board’s recommendations are non-binding. The official framework page was last updated on 25 August 2026.

proposedRecord.content: Queensland’s current QGEA artificial intelligence governance policy is Policy v2.0.0, Current/Mandated and effective from August 2026. It requires covered agencies to establish AI governance arrangements with regard to the current version of ISO 38507. Agencies must align with Australia’s AI Ethics Principles by preparing a Foundational AI Risk Assessment (FAIRA), or an agreed equivalent, as evidence of a structured assessment of transparency, accountability and risk across the AI lifecycle. The policy applies to Queensland Government departments and also to specified accountable officers and statutory bodies. The official page was last updated on 26 August 2026.

The landing page offers https://www.digital.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/2026-10/AI-Architecture-ACCESSIBLE.pdf and https://www.digital.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/2026-10/AI-Architecture-Companion-Guide-ACCESSIBLE.pdf, each marked last updated 23 Oct 2026. proposedRecord.description: OVIC guidance setting minimum privacy and information-security expectations for Victorian public sector organisations adopting enterprise generative AI tools.

source.title: Use of enterprise Generative AI tools in the Victorian public sector

reviewedDate.notes: Rechecked 5 Nov 2026: the OVIC page states 'Last updated 26 June 2026'. Unchanged from the verified record's amended date.

agencies: Office of the Victorian Information Commissioner
proposedRecord.content: From Monday 12 September 2020, OVIC's website will no longer be supported in Internet Explorer (IE). We recommend installing Microsoft Edge, Google Chrome, Safari, Firefox, or Opera to visit the site. Use of enterprise Generative AI tools in the Victorian public sector Last updated 26 June 2026 This guidance outlines the Office of the Victorian Information Commissioner’s (OVIC) minimum expectations for Victorian public sector organisations (VPS organisations) using enterprise Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) tools.1 It also sets out the key information privacy and information security obligations for VPS organisations to consider. Generative AI is a type of Artificial Intelligence that creates content, such as text, images, music, audio and video. Generative AI tools do this by predicting the best response to the information entered, known as a prompt. Predictions, also known as outputs, are made based on the content of the prompt and the data on which the Generative AI tool has been trained.2 This guidance relates to Generative AI tools that are purchased at an enterprise level, and operate within a VPS organisation’s securely managed environment. Enterprise Generative AI tools are integrated within an organisation’s existing systems. Examples include tenanted versions of Microsoft 365 Copilot, Chat GPT Enterprise, Duet AI for Google Workspace, Zoom IQ and Slack GPT. 3 The adoption and use of Generative AI tools may magnify existing information privacy and information security risks for VPS organisations, and create new ones (some examples are included below). VPS organisations should therefore take the steps outlined below to improve their information security maturity and privacy practices before adopting an enterprise Generative AI tool.4 The risks involved in using publicly available Generative AI tools are different to those involved in using enterprise Generative AI tools. For guidance on using publicly available Generative AI tools, please refer to OVIC’s guidance on the use of personal information with publicly available Generative AI tools in the Victorian public sector. OVIC’s minimum expectations This section sets out OVIC’s minimum expectations for VPS organisations to work through prior to purchasing and integrating an enterprise Generative AI tool. VPS organisations should: Assess the maturity of their existing information security program,5 including: identifying existing information holdings and systems that may be impacted by the introduction of an integrated Generative AI tool, including due consideration of their security value considering how any Generative AI outputs will be assessed, valued and securely managed, including applying appropriate protective markings for newly generated information assets conducting a security risk assessment for the integration of an enterprise Generative AI tool, including due consideration of adjusted risk profiles and development of treatment plans to address relevant Generative AI features implementing any updated treatment plans by rolling out new or changed controls, including consideration of the organisation’s existing logical access controls implementing a formal process for the ongoing monitoring and review of risks and controls. This is especially important given the dynamic development and release of enhancements and new features in Generative AI tools. Undertake privacy impact assessments (PIAs) to understand the ways in which the enterprise Generative AI tool will be utilised, the risks it presents to the privacy of individuals, whether and how those risks can be mitigated, and in light of any residual risks, the extent to which it is appropriate to proceed to purchase the tool.6 There may be high-risk functions or specific business units within a VPS organisation for whom it is not appropriate to use a Generative AI tool.7 Ensure that risks and controls are regularly reviewed and monitored. Be careful when using Generative AI tools in ways that may significantly impact one or more individuals. This includes automated decision-making and the use of these tools during earlier steps in a decision-making process, where that earlier use significantly influences or materially assists the organisation in making its decision. Earlier steps may include using a Generative AI tool to conduct research, summarise key information, facts or evidence or make a prediction, recommendation, assessment, summary, conclusion or inference. Using Generative AI tools in decision-making processes carries privacy risks under Victoria’s Information Privacy Principles (IPPs). This includes IPP 2 risks (where personal information is used for a secondary purpose that is not permitted), IPP 3 risks (poor data quality and accuracy) and IPP 1 risks (the collection of personal information may not be considered fair if collected for use in fully automated decision-making that significantly impacts on the individual). Ensure that settings can be configured to enhance information privacy and information security, such as disabling or limiting data sharing between certain platforms and between the VPS organisation and the company that owns the enterprise Generative AI tool. Develop organisational policies on the use of Generative AI tools, and communicate about the policies to staff, contracted service providers and other personnel. Develop and implement clear and tailored guidance and training for their staff, contracted service providers and other personnel on the use of the enterprise Generative AI tool, that: covers how to safely and responsibly use the enterprise Generative AI tool, prompt engineering, risk assessment and management, human review of generated outputs, and active monitoring and reviews to identify potential misuse ensures all users of the enterprise Generative AI tool are aware of and understand what information they are permitted to enter into the enterprise Generative AI tool and its permitted use cases ensures all users of the enterprise Generative AI tool are aware of how the tool may generate, collect, use or disclose personal information and public sector information, and understand how to ensure the accuracy and security of the information. Develop an incident response plan for dealing with inadvertent or unauthorised disclosures, access or misuse of information through the enterprise Generative AI tool. VPS organisations are responsible for all actions and content generated by the enterprise Generative AI tool they use. Where an information security incident or interference with privacy occurs through the use of the tool, VPS organisations will not be able to simply say that the incident or interference was caused by AI. Notify OVIC of information privacy and information security incidents, in line with the Information Security Incident Notification Scheme.8 Information privacy requirements This section applies to VPS organisations covered by Part 3 of the Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014 (PDP Act). The 10 Information Privacy Principles (IPPs), as set out in Schedule 1 of the PDP Act, will apply to the collection and handling of personal information that may be entered into, generated, or used by an enterprise Generative AI tool.9 While all 10 IPPs are relevant to the handling of personal information by an organisation, IPPs 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 will be most relevant when integrating an enterprise Generative AI tool.10 Collection of personal information IPP 1 sets out that an organisation must only collect personal information if it is necessary to fulfill one or more of its functions. The collection must be lawful, fair and not unreasonably intrusive. Organisations must also provide notice to individuals about why the information is being collected, how it will be used and how individuals can access the information. Organisations should understand that when an enterprise Generative AI tool generates new content in response to a user prompt (such as “draft me a summary of the main points in the document called ‘John Smith’s CV’”), this generated content constitutes a new collection of personal information. Organisations must comply with the requirements of IPP 1. Example – Collection of personal information via a collaboration platform An organisation’s HR team invites a Senior Operations Manager to a meeting via a collaboration platform to provide an update on an internal conduct investigation involving one of the manager’s staff. The manager realises at the last minute that they cannot attend, so asks the enterprise Generative AI tool within the collaboration platform to ‘follow’ the meeting so they can receive a recap of what was discussed. The HR team joins the meeting and see a message from the manager that they can no longer attend. They decide that without the manager, there is no point discussing the matter but, since they have all set aside 30 minutes for the meeting, they use the time to instead discuss another matter, relating to a different staff member’s request for family violence leave. The next day, the manager sends a prompt to the enterprise Generative AI tool within the collaboration platform, asking “what were the main points discussed at the meeting?”. The enterprise Generative AI tool responds with a summary of the details about the other staff member and their request for family violence leave. The generation of the summary content by the enterprise Generative AI tool is a collection of personal information, which would likely contravene at least IPP 1.1 (as the manager had no need to know that information). Use and disclosure of personal information IPP 2 provides that personal information may only be used or disclosed for the primary purpose for which it is was collected, or where an exception applies under IPPs 2.1(a-h). Human error is the leading cause of data breaches reported to OVIC involving unauthorised use and disclosure of personal information. Without proper controls in place, the implementation of an enterprise Generative AI tool could exacerbate this, given the increased speed at which personal information can be generated, used, and disclosed. While users are in control of what they do with content generated by an enterprise Generative AI tool, there is a risk that humans using a tool described as ‘intelligent’ may not always exercise an appropriate level of scrutiny over its output. Further, as enterprise Generative AI tools use documents from an organisation’s information holdings to generate content in response to a user prompt, they could provide the user with personal information with which they were previously unfamiliar (even if access controls are correctly configured and the user has a right to know this information). This creates a risk that VPS employees could be unaware of the original purpose for which the personal information was collected, and cannot properly consider whether a proposed use or disclosure would comply with IPP 2. Example – Unauthorised disclosure of personal information generated by an enterprise Generative AI tool An organisation’s Assessment Officer wants to write a letter rejecting Person A’s application for a service. They prompt their enterprise Generative AI tool to draft this letter and base it off a letter they wrote two months ago rejecting Person B’s application. Impressed by how quickly the enterprise Generative AI tool drafts the six-page letter, the Assessment Officer quickly reads through and digitally signs it. They then send the letter to Person A by email. Person A later calls the Complaints Officer and informs them that while the letter was addressed to Person A, it also contained the name of Person B in the body of the letter as well as other personal information relating to Person B’s application. As well as highlighting an interference with Person B’s privacy, Person A also suspects that the Assessment Officer may have based their decision on the wrong personal information, and asks that their application is considered afresh. The disclosure of Person B’s personal information to Person A is a breach of IPP 2. The use of inaccurate personal information about Person A would also likely breach IPP 3, relating to accuracy of personal information (see discussion below). Additionally, this scenario raises concerns about the fairness of the decision made. Accuracy of personal information IPP 3 requires an organisation to take reasonable steps to ensure the personal information it collects, uses or discloses is accurate, complete and up to date. The use of an enterprise Generative AI tool presents an increased risk of organisations generating, using or disclosing inaccurate personal information. This is because Generative AI outputs will not always give the correct information. They simply make predictions based on the prompt they receive and the training they’ve had. Further, where a user re-generates the same prompt, the Generative AI tool likely won’t reproduce the original output. In choosing whether to implement an enterprise Generative AI tool, organisations should assess whether they will be able to mitigate risks associated with the generation of inaccurate, incomplete or outdated personal information. Example – Summary of complaint documents present incomplete picture A complainant makes a complaint to a regulator about the actions of a government department. In a 20-page document, the complainant sets out comprehensive details of their allegations, the serious harm they have experienced, and what they want the department to do to resolve their concerns, including payment of $20,000 in compensation. The complaint is assigned to a Complaint Officer at the regulator’s office. After reading the complaint once, the Officer writes a prompt to an enterprise Generative AI tool asking it to summarise the content into a new document, and directs that it should be two pages long. Once generated, the Officer emails the summary to the department asking for its response to the complaint. The department responds, agreeing that the conduct occurred as alleged but insists that it was a trivial matter that had little impact on the complainant. The department offers $1,000 in compensation to resolve the complaint. The complainant rejects this, and the regulator closes the complaint on the basis that it cannot be resolved. The complainant is disappointed by the department’s approach and asks the Complaint Officer how a government body could read her complaint and still place so little value on what she went through. The Officer explains that it was actually an AI-generated summary of the complaint that was sent to the department, and provides the complainant with a copy. The complainant is shocked when they read the summary. They believe it has omitted crucial elements of their allegations, and has minimised their description of the harm suffered. They believe it has created an inaccurate and incomplete description of the complaint, and has led to the department trivialising their experience and dismissing the complaint. The collection and use of inaccurate personal information about the complainant would likely breach IPP 3, as the regulator has not taken reasonable steps to make sure that the personal information it collects, uses or discloses is accurate and complete. Security of personal information IPP 4 requires an organisation to take reasonable steps to protect the personal information it holds from misuse, loss, and unauthorised access, modification and disclosure. The adoption of an enterprise Generative AI tool could magnify existing risks to the security of personal information for organisations. One particular risk relates to unauthorised access to information, where access permissions have not been properly configured within other organisational systems that are then integrated with the enterprise Generative AI tool. Misconfiguration of access controls is one of the most common causes of data breaches reported to OVIC.11 Organisations should review and update access controls for any platforms integrated with enterprise Generative AI tools. Further information on steps organisations should take in relation to security controls is covered in the next section. Example – Unauthorised access due to misconfigured access controls A manager is drafting an internal document for a new member of their team to explain the basics of performance development procedures. Looking for inspiration, the manager prompts an enterprise Generative AI tool, asking about any previous documents relating to performance development that other staff in the organisation have created. Due to an access control misconfiguration, of which the manager was unaware, the Generative AI tool sends the manager a range of documents that include final copies of the Performance Development Plans of their colleagues. The disclosure of the Performance Development Plans of other colleagues to the manager due to misconfigured access controls would likely be a breach of IPP 4.1. Privacy policies IPP 5 requires VPS organisations to have a privacy policy, outlining how they handle the personal information they hold. Where personal information is handled by an enterprise Generative AI tool, a VPS organisation’s privacy policy should be clear about this. This is especially important where the outputs of an enterprise Generative AI tool are used to inform decision making about an individual, such as whether they are eligible for a service or a payment. Information security requirements Before VPS organisations implement any enterprise Generative AI tool, the public sector body head must assess the information security risks to the confidentiality, integrity and availability of public sector information and systems proposed to be used by the enterprise Generative AI tool,12 and ensure adherence to the Victorian Protective Data Security Standards (the Standards).13 The Standards set out the mandatory requirements to protect public sector information across all security domains including governance, information, personnel, information communications technology and physical security. The PDP Act extends these information security obligations to contracted service providers (CSPs), requiring public sector body heads to ensure that a CSP does not do an act or engage in a practice that contravenes a Standard.14 VPS organisations therefore must ensure their security risk assessment includes an evaluation of CSPs relevant to the enterprise Generative AI tool. By following this approach organisations: will be best placed to understand the risks of an enterprise Generative AI tool within the context of their organisation and risk profile will ensure that any changes to their operating environment (people, processes and technology) are incorporated into existing risk assessments provide the public sector body head with full visibility and understanding of current risks associated with an enterprise Generative AI tool following any changes. For the purpose of this guidance, VPS organisations are organisations subject to Parts 3 and 4 of the Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014. See sections 3 and 84 of that Act for a list of organisations covered by these Parts.For further information on Generative AI concepts, see the resource developed by the Centre of Excellence for Automated Decision-Making and Society, and OVIC. This guidance replaces the guidance OVIC issued in its public statement on the use of Microsoft 365 Copilot in the Victorian public sector in October 2023.OVIC recommends that VPS organisations review OVIC’s guidance on engaging third party providers prior to purchasing an enterprise Generative AI tool. The guidance outlines the steps VPS organisations should take to ensure they meet their information privacy and information security obligations. See the information security requirements section below.OVIC has a PIA template and accompanying guide available to assist organisations to undertake a PIA. It likely will not be sufficient for one overarching PIA to be undertaken on the integration of the enterprise Generative AI tool. PIAs should be conducted for individual functions or uses of the enterprise Generative AI tool, or by business unit, where a business unit will use the Generative AI tool for a discrete, defined purpose.Incidents can be reported via OVIC’s incident notification form. Personal information is defined in section 3 of the Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014 as ‘information or an opinion… that is recorded in any form and whether true or not, about an individual whose identity is apparent, or can reasonably be ascertained, from the information or opinion’. The definition of personal information excludes health information, which is covered by the Health Records Act 2001.For guidance on how to interpret and apply the IPPs, refer to OVIC’s Guidelines to the Information Privacy Principles. OVIC Incidents Insights Report: 1 July 2022 – 31 December 2022. Public sector data, also known as public sector information, is defined in section 3 of the PDP Act as ‘information (including personal information) obtained, received or held by an agency or body to which Part 4 applies’.The Victorian Protective Data Security Standards are available on OVIC’s website. Section 88(2), PDP Act. proposedRecord.content: ASIC media release 26-226MR is dated 24 September 2026 on the page (displayDate). It announces amendments to the ASIC Market Integrity Rules (Securities Markets) 2017 and the ASIC Market Integrity Rules (Futures Markets) 2017 that modernise trading-systems obligations for algorithmic trading, including AI and machine learning, require participants to test, monitor and govern trading systems and algorithms, align more closely with IOSCO principles, apply trading-system requirements consistently to manually entered and automated orders, and clarify the false or misleading appearance rule for AI-enabled and other trading. The release says the amendments follow Consultation Paper 386 and take effect in 2028 after an 18-month transition. The release does not mention a kill switch or a seven-year record-keeping period. ASIC consultation CS 63 states Released 24 September 2026 and that comments close at 5 pm AEDT on 5 November 2026. It states that the market integrity rules were amended in September 2026 and that the rules commence on 18 March 2028 after an 18-month transition. It proposes updates to RG 265 and RG 266 and moving relevant guidance from RG 241 into those guides so RG 241 can be retired. The CS 63 page does not mention a kill switch or seven-year record keeping. Attachments 5 and 6, the marked-up compilations of the securities and futures rules, state that the changes are in force from 18 March 2028 and that market participants and market operators can continue to comply with the rules as in force on 15 October 2024 until 18 March 2028. The Federal Register of Legislation records ASIC Market Integrity Rules (Securities Markets) Amendment Instrument 2026/574 (F2026L01223) and ASIC Market Integrity Rules (Futures Markets) Amendment Instrument 2026/575 (F2026L01224). Each instrument is dated 15 September 2026 and was registered on 17 September 2026. Section 2 of each instrument states that it commences on the day that is 18 months after the day it is registered. The instruments do not use the term kill switch. They do set seven-year record obligations in the amended trading-system rules. In the securities instrument, a trading participant must maintain records of trading messages identified under the monitoring and post-trade surveillance rule, and any measures taken, for seven years from the date of the relevant trading message (rule 5.6.3A(3)); maintain records that demonstrate compliance with the trading-algorithm controls and testing obligations for seven years (rule 5.6.3B(4)); and document and retain for at least seven years records of the methodology, scope and results of the Initial Certification Review (rule 5.6.4(4)), the Material Change Review (rule 5.6.8(4)) and the Annual Review (rule 5.6.8A(5)), and of recommended changes applied as a result. The futures instrument states the corresponding obligations in rules 2.2B.3(3), 2.2B.4(4), 2.2B.5(4), 2.2B.8(4) and 2.2B.9(5).

proposedRecord.title: Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2026-28
proposedRecord.description: Australian Federal Police strategy for a human-led, responsible approach to adopting AI in policing from 2026 to 2028. It sets five strategic goals and four adoption pillars: People, Process, Technology and Partnerships.
proposedRecord.content:
The Australian Federal Police (AFP) publishes the Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2026-28 on its publication page, with a PDF of the strategy. In her foreword, Commissioner Krissy Barrett APM says the strategy commits the AFP to a human-led, responsible and transparent approach to AI, that AI will support, not replace, the judgement of AFP members, and that accountability for decisions always rests with the AFP.

Vision: to establish the AFP as a collaborative leader that brings law enforcement and the broader AI community together in applied responsible use of AI.

Strategic goals: counter the criminal threat from AI, including deepfakes, synthetic media and disinformation; strengthen data-driven decision making; safeguard member wellbeing by reducing exposure to harmful material such as child abuse material; empower creativity and workforce engagement; and enhance productivity through services such as transcription, translation, summarisation, video analytics and entity recognition.

Adoption pillars: People (AI knowledge, culture and leadership; human-led decision-making; safeguarding member wellbeing), Process (responsible AI governance and policies; operational alignment), Technology (investment in technology; end-to-end data management) and Partnerships (partnership and collaboration; public trust and transparency).

The AFP says it has fully adopted the guiding principles of the ANZPAA Responsible and Ethical Artificial Intelligence Framework: transparency, explainability, accountability, human oversight, fairness, skills and knowledge, proportionality and justifiability, reliability, and privacy and security. The strategy also names Australia's AI Ethics Principles, the National Framework for the Assurance of AI in Government, the Policy for the Responsible Use of AI in Government and the Voluntary AI Safety Standard as informing its approach.

The risks it names are AI system failure; overuse, inappropriate or reckless use; legal, ethical and privacy risk; reputational and public trust risk; and bias and hallucination. It says the AFP will establish mechanisms to measure progress across all strategic pillars. The strategy gives no specific measures.
proposedRecord.aiSummary: The AFP strategy for 2026 to 2028 commits the agency to human-led, responsible AI use. It sets five goals and four pillars, adopts the ANZPAA police AI principles, and says AI will support, not replace, the judgement of AFP members.

proposedRecord.content: The Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026 was introduced and read a first time in the House of Representatives on 15 October 2026, and the second reading was moved that day. On 28 October 2026 the bill home page records that the second reading was agreed, that consideration in detail agreed 15 government amendments and 8 crossbench amendments, and that the third reading was agreed. Status remains proposed: the register has no separate before-Parliament status, and the bill is not an Act. The same page's Status field still reads "Before Reps" and it shows no Senate progress table. The page records referral on 15 October 2026 to the Senate Environment and Communications Legislation Committee, with a report due on 20 November 2026. That reporting date is stored as scheduled_review because the register has no committee-report date type. It is the committee's reporting date, not a statutory review of an Act. Divisions listed on the bill home page for 28 October 2026 include the question that the amendments moved by Ms Chaney be agreed to. The sheet linked from that page (Kate Chaney MP) proposes inserting paragraph 25E(1)(da), "material or conduct that simulates emotional intimacy and encourages or fosters a child's dependence on it in place of human relationships". The third-reading PDF was not readable in this capture, so that sentence is the circulated sheet, not a quotation from the text as agreed. As described in the approved 11–17 October 2026 signal, the bill covers services that generate material using AI (s 25B(1)(h)), requires yearly risk assessments, and in Schedule 3 would repeal the online-safety industry codes and standards 12 months after Royal Assent. Those codes remain in force on esafety-genai-industry-codes. An exposure draft was released for targeted consultation on 8 September 2026 (Minister for Communications). The Minister announced introduction on 15 October 2026. The department has a page on the digital duty of care.

proposedRecord.content:
The Online Safety and Other Legislation Amendment (My Face, My Rights) Bill 2025 is a private senator's bill sponsored by Senator David Pocock, introduced in the Senate.

The bill home page summary says it amends the Online Safety Act 2021 to establish a complaints and enforcement regime for the non-consensual sharing of digitally altered or artificially generated audio or visual content that depicts a person's face or voice without their consent (deepfake material), and amends the Privacy Act 1988 to establish a cause of action for the wrongful use or disclosure of deepfake material.

Progress in the Senate: introduced and read a first time on 24 November 2025; second reading moved on 24 November 2025; second reading debate on 25 June 2026. On 5 November 2026 the bill home page shows its status as Before Senate, with no proposed amendments circulated. It is not law.

The Online Safety and Other Legislation Amendment (My Face, My Rights) Bill 2025 is a private senator's bill sponsored by Senator David Pocock, introduced in the Senate.

The bill home page summary says it amends the Online Safety Act 2021 to establish a complaints and enforcement regime for the non-consensual sharing of digitally altered or artificially generated audio or visual content that depicts a person's face or voice without their consent (deepfake material), and amends the Privacy Act 1988 to establish a cause of action for the wrongful use or disclosure of deepfake material.

Progress in the Senate: introduced and read a first time on 24 November 2025; second reading moved on 24 November 2025; second reading debate on 25 June 2026. On 5 November 2026 the bill home page shows its status as Before Senate, with no proposed amendments circulated. It is not law.

proposedRecord.content: From Monday 12 September 2020, OVIC's website will no longer be supported in Internet Explorer (IE). We recommend installing Microsoft Edge, Google Chrome, Safari, Firefox, or Opera to visit the site. Use of publicly available Generative AI tools in the Victorian public sector Last updated 26 June 2026 This guidance outlines the Office of the Victorian Information Commissioner’s (OVIC) position on the use of publicly available Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) tools within Victorian public sector organisations (VPS organisations).1 Generative AI is a type of Artificial Intelligence that creates content, such as text, images, music, audio and video. Generative AI tools do this by predicting the best response to the information entered, known as a prompt. Predictions, also known as outputs, are made based on the content of the prompt and the data on which the Generative AI tool has been trained.2 This guidance relates to VPS organisations’ use of any Generative AI tool that is publicly available.3 Publicly available Generative AI tools are platforms or software that can be accessed via a web browser or application. Generally, publicly available tools have minimal controls for how the information entered is used or protected. At the time of issuing this guidance, examples include free versions of ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Grammarly, Claude, Perplexity, Otter, QuillBot and Llama.4 The risks involved in using publicly available Generative AI tools are different to those involved in using tools that are purchased at an enterprise level. For guidance on using enterprise Generative AI tools in a secure environment, please refer to OVIC’s guidance on the use of enterprise Generative AI tools in the Victorian public sector. Personal information and publicly available Generative AI tools VPS organisations should ensure their staff, contracted service providers and other personnel do not enter personal information into publicly available Generative AI tools.5 Doing so will likely be a contravention of the Information Privacy Principles (IPPs) in the Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014 (PDP Act), and may cause significant harm to individuals whose information is used in publicly available Generative AI tools.6 Generative AI outputs can also reveal or create personal information. Personal information includes opinions about individuals. VPS organisations must treat outputs that contain personal information as a collection of personal information, and handle the information in accordance with the IPPs.7 Public sector information and publicly available Generative AI tools VPS organisations should ensure their staff, contracted service providers and other personnel limit the public sector information that is entered into publicly available Generative AI tools.8 VPS organisations should only enter public sector information that is already publicly known or approved for public release.9 The risk of using publicly available Generative AI tools with public sector information is context specific, and will differ depending on the Generative AI tool and its intended use. Risks of using publicly available Generative AI tools Using personal information with a publicly available Generative AI tool raises significant information privacy and other concerns. Some examples are outlined below. Disclosure of personal information: using personal information with a publicly available Generative AI tool may mean disclosing that information to the company that owns the tool. The information may be subsequently used, disclosed or accessed for unauthorised purposes unrelated to the original prompt. This may contravene IPPs 2.1 and 4.1, relating to use and disclosure of personal information, and information security.The information entered into a publicly available Generative AI tool is likely to be stored outside Victoria, and in many cases, in jurisdictions that do not have information privacy and information security laws equivalent to the PDP Act. This may contravene IPP 9, relating to transborder data flows. Collection of personal information: generating personal information with a Generative AI tool constitutes a new collection of personal information. VPS organisations should be mindful of the necessity, lawfulness and fairness of collecting new personal information in this way. This may result in inaccurate information or opinions being generated and subsequently used or disclosed, which may contravene IPPs 1.1, 1.2, 3.1 and 10, relating to the collection of personal information, data quality, and sensitive information. IPP 1.3, which requires VPS organisations to provide a notice of collection to individuals when their personal information is collected, will also be relevant. It will be difficult for VPS organisations to provide adequate notice, where at the time of collection it is not known that personal information will be used with publicly available Generative AI tools, resulting in its disclosure and further use. Further, providing notice of collection where personal information is created by a publicly available Generative AI tool and therefore collected by the VPS organisation, may be difficult. Accuracy of information: it can be difficult to ensure the accuracy of personal information, for both that which is entered into a Generative AI tool and generated by it. Generative AI tools are not a reliable source of accurate information. They simply make predictions based on the prompt they receive and the training they’ve had. Relying on outputs that contain personal information may contravene IPP 3 in relation to data quality. Information accuracy issues also apply to non-personal information that is generated by a Generative AI tool. Information security: publicly available Generative AI tools raise a number of information security issues. For example, unauthorised disclosure of and access to personal information and other public sector information by third parties, which could lead to a contravention of IPP 4.1 and the Victorian Protective Data Security Standards.10 This could lead to harm to individuals and VPS organisations, if the information is used for malicious intent. Retention of personal information: information entered into a publicly available Generative AI tool may be retained indefinitely by the company that owns the tool. Once information is entered into a publicly available Generative AI tool, it may not be possible to extract that information, leaving the VPS organisation without the ability to adhere to IPP 4.2. Generative AI tools are trained on vast amounts of data, including in many cases, information entered by a user.11 Retaining this information is of benefit to the companies that own these tools, but where personal information is involved, may contravene IPP 4.2 relating to data destruction. VPS organisations also have obligations under the Public Records Act 1973 that must be adhered to.12 Fairness: Publicly available Generative AI tools should not be used to formulate decisions, undertake assessments, or for other administrative functions that may have consequences for individuals. The use of these tools with personal information may cause significant harm to those individuals whose information has been used. It risks unfair decisions being made about them based on information created by Generative AI, that may be inaccurate or of a diminished quality. For information on other privacy risks associated with using generative AI in decision-making processes, please refer to OVIC’s guidance on the use of enterprise Generative AI tools in the Victorian public sector. OVIC’s minimum expectations For VPS organisations using, or considering using, publicly available Generative AI tools, OVIC expects at a minimum they will: conduct security risk assessments before use, in accordance with their risk management framework to ensure that any risks are identified, assessed, treated and monitored accordingly13 implement a formal process for the ongoing monitoring and review of risks and controls review the publicly available Generative AI tools’ terms and conditions prior to use, and where possible, configure security settings to protect public sector information only permit public sector information that is already publicly known or approved for public release to be used with publicly available Generative AI tools require their staff, contracted service providers and other personnel to check the accuracy of generated content before using it develop organisational policies on the use of Generative AI tools, and communicate about the policies to staff, contracted service providers and other personnel train staff on how to safely and responsibly use Generative AI tools, including for what purposes publicly available Generative AI tools may be used, which tools are permitted, and what information is appropriate to enter into a publicly available Generative AI tool notify OVIC if personal information or public sector information that is not already publicly known or approved for public release has been used with a publicly available Generative AI tool.14 VPS organisations are welcome to contact OVIC for guidance on managing the information privacy and information security impacts of publicly available Generative AI tools. OVIC can be contacted at enquiries@ovic.vic.gov.au. Scenarios The following scenarios have been prepared to illustrate the risks involved with using personal information in publicly available Generative AI tools. Scenario 1 – Entering and generating content A hiring manager is using a publicly available Generative AI tool to generate content for a recruitment selection report. They enter the CVs and interview notes captured by the panel, and the reference reports of five candidates into the Generative AI tool. They prompt the tool to generate six paragraphs recommending Candidate A for the role. Trainers at the overseas company that owns the Generative AI tool subsequently review the content and prompt used with the tool, which is used to improve the model. This results in a disclosure of the personal information of five individuals, in contravention of IPP 2.1 and 4.1. As the content is stored outside of Victoria and retained by the company indefinitely, it is also a contravention of IPP 9 and IPP 4.2. Scenario 2 – Using a publicly available Generative AI tool for decision making A Victorian public sector employee is writing a report evaluating whether a prisoner should be granted parole, and uses a publicly available Generative AI tool to generate the content of the report, including the evaluation of risks. In doing so, they enter the prisoner’s personal information. The company that owns the Generative AI tool stores its data outside of Australia. The Generative AI tool generates an output in response to the prompt. The employee does not carry out their own independent evaluation and relies solely on the information contained in the output. The employee then submits the recommendation to their supervisor that the prisoner’s parole application be rejected. The employee’s supervisor reviews the report and notes that the reasoning for the opinion rejecting the parole application is flawed, and that the wrong recommendation had been reached. The supervisor rewrites the report themselves, undertaking analysis of the information to ensure its accuracy, and resubmits the report. If it had not been for the supervisor’s intervention, the use of the Generative AI tool could have had severe negative consequences for the prisoner. As the employee used a publicly available Generative AI tool, the information they entered into the tool resulted in an unauthorised disclosure of information. The use of the personal and sensitive information of the prisoner would contravene IPPs 2.1, 3.1, 4.1 and 9 at a minimum. Scenario 3 – Using a publicly available Generative AI tool in a public school A teacher uses a publicly available Generative AI tool to generate an email to a student’s parents, expressing their concern about the student’s behaviour and academic performance. In doing so, the teacher enters the notes they have taken about the student across the term to generate the output. The company that owns the Generative AI tool stores its data outside of Australia. The teacher isn’t happy with the tone of the output, so generates it again. In doing so, the Generative AI tool generates a new output with a different tone and different opinion about the student. The teacher then sends the content in an email to the student’s parents. The parents receive the email and raise concerns with the teacher about the opinions formed about their child, and question who wrote the letter. The teacher explains they used a Generative AI tool to generate the content. The parents are not satisfied the generation of the content about their child was necessary, and consider the use of the tool to be an unreasonably intrusive method of collecting information about their child. As generating personal information using a Generative AI tool is considered a new ‘collection’ of personal information, there has been a contravention of IPPs 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3. Given the student’s personal information was entered into a publicly available Generative AI tool, where data is stored outside Victoria, a contravention of IPPs 4.1 and 9 has also occurred. For the purpose of this guidance, VPS organisations are organisations subject to Part 3 of the Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014. See section 3 of that Act for a list of organisations.For further information on Generative AI concepts, see the resource developed by the Centre of Excellence for Automated Decision-Making and Society, and OVIC. This guidance replaces the guidance OVIC issued in its public statement on the use of personal information with ChatGPT in February 2024.The Australian Government and the Victorian Government have both issued a ban on DeepSeek.Personal information is defined in section 3 of the Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014 as ‘information or an opinion… that is recorded in any form and whether true or not, about an individual whose identity is apparent, or can reasonably be ascertained, from the information or opinion’. The definition of personal information excludes health information, which is covered by the Health Records Act 2001.In November 2024, OVIC published a report on its investigation into the use of ChatGPT by a Child Protection worker. The report highlights a range of information privacy issues that stemmed from personal information being entered into a publicly available Generative AI tool. Comprehensive Guidelines to the Information Privacy Principles are available on OVIC’s website. Public sector data, also known as public sector information, is defined in section 3 of the PDP Act as ‘information (including personal information) obtained, received or held by an agency or body to which Part 4 applies’. Not all VPS organisations will have obligations under Part 4 of the PDP Act. However, OVIC recommends all VPS organisations limit the information they enter into publicly available Generative AI tools.This is consistent with the position taken in the Victorian Government’s Administrative guideline on the safe and responsible use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Victorian public sector. Bodies that are subject to Part 4 of the Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014 must comply with the Victorian Protective Data Security Standards. Some Generative AI tools provide users with the ability to disable the information they enter from being recorded, and opt-out of the information they enter being used to train the tool. Even if these features are disabled, privacy concerns around the disclosure of personal information and unauthorised access remain.For further information on AI and recordkeeping, refer to the Public Record Office Victoria’s guidance and policy. OVIC recommends that VPS organisations also conduct privacy impact assessments (PIAs) where a program or initiative involves the handling of personal information. As this guidance states that no personal information should be entered into publicly available Generative AI tools, PIAs will not be necessary if no personal information is handled. For guidance on PIAs, refer to OVIC’s website. VPS organisations should report information privacy and information security incidents to OVIC via the incident notification form. proposedRecord.content: ASD's ACSC publication. The page is dated 05 Nov 2026 and last reviewed 05 Nov 2026. It explains what open-weight AI models are: models whose weights are publicly released so an organisation can download, modify and operate them on its own infrastructure, typically without the training data, training code or full documentation. It describes benefits of local control, including hosting in the organisation's own environment (including disconnected environments), choosing when to adopt updates, and configuring safeguards under the organisation's own governance. It says those benefits sit with greater responsibility for security, monitoring, maintenance and incident response. Risk areas on the page, which arise because released weights can be copied, modified and redistributed without the original developer's oversight, are model selection, provenance and developer jurisdiction; model, data and software supply chain (including executable model formats and hidden behaviour); fine-tuned model security (memorisation and theft of sensitive training information); and safeguards, integrations and agentic systems (outdated, weakened or removed safeguards, prompt injection and unauthorised tool use). Recommended actions include defining intended and prohibited uses, not adopting a model whose provenance cannot be established for that use, obtaining artefacts only from assessed sources, verifying hashes and signatures, sandboxing new models, preferring formats that cannot contain executable code, treating fine-tuned files as potentially containing the data used to create them, and placing controls outside the model, with human approval for high-risk or irreversible actions. The audience is executives, technology leaders and cyber security practitioners considering whether to adopt open-weight models. It points to the companion publication Selecting, deploying and operating open-weight AI models securely, and to ASD's Careful adoption of agentic AI services and Agentic AI harnesses for agentic deployments. Announced at https://www.cyber.gov.au/news/new-guidance-on-open-weight-ai-models. Staged for editorial review; not verified.

proposedRecord.content: ASD's ACSC companion publication. The page shows 05 Nov 2026 twice, in the published and last-reviewed positions. It assumes the organisation has decided, or is close to deciding, to operate an open-weight model itself, and covers the responsibilities that creates. It distinguishes local deployment (on infrastructure the organisation controls, on-premises or in a public cloud) from consuming a hosted API or a third party that operates the model, and says a hosted open-weight service should be treated like other hosted AI or cloud services. Governance on the page: an organisational policy for approved use cases, security requirements, accountability and risk acceptance; a formal onboarding assessment; a register of approved models (use case, owner, risk acceptance, next review) and a technical inventory of versions, artefacts, adapters, dependencies and configurations; and processes to reassess after material change and to update, replace or retire models. Selection and operation principles on the page are: choose proportionately; know and verify the source (including provenance, licence, modifications, and country of origin as one factor rather than proof of trustworthiness); verify suitability by independent testing of the specific version; assess and secure the deployment before committing to a design, including egress and controls outside the model; and maintain assurance, including what the organisation must monitor itself when vendor support is limited. Deployment risks, which the page says the operating organisation manages without a provider's monitoring and incident response, are deployment and infrastructure security (segmentation, separate development and production, authentication, multi-factor authentication for administrative access, least privilege, controlled outbound access, rate limits, and tested containment); model maintenance and updates (track releases and advisories, test before deployment, keep rollback, reassess unmaintained models); and monitoring, evaluation and incident response (log access, prompts, responses and tool activity commensurate with risk, watch for misuse, theft, leakage and safeguard bypass, and keep tested rollback, credential revocation and incident reporting). The audience is executives, technology leaders and cyber security practitioners responsible for these models. Companion: Open-weight AI models: Opportunities and cyber security risks. Announced at https://www.cyber.gov.au/news/new-guidance-on-open-weight-ai-models. Staged for editorial review; not verified.

proposedRecord.title: A Digital Detox: Education Ministers’ decisions on technology and generative AI in schools
proposedRecord.description: Decisions of the Education Ministers Meeting, published by the Department of Education on 4 November 2026, restricting student use of generative AI in primary schools and in secondary assessments, with timing, scope and application set by each jurisdiction or sector.
proposedRecord.content:
On 4 November 2026 the Department of Education published "A Digital Detox", a paper setting out decisions of the Education Ministers Meeting. The announcement page is dated 4 November 2026. The paper says ministers adopted the policy at their meeting on 2 November 2026.

In the section "The next steps: digital detox", ministers agreed to restrict student use of generative AI applications in primary schools, recognising this may involve the continued use of some AI features built into technologies currently in use, with the timing, scope and application of potential limits to be determined by each jurisdiction or sector.

Ministers agreed to restrict student use of generative AI in secondary school assessments, with the same timing, scope and application caveat for each jurisdiction or sector.

Ministers agreed to introduce, trial or consider limits for screen use in schools, again with timing, scope and application determined by each jurisdiction or sector.

Ministers agreed to establish the Australian Schools Digital Detox Taskforce to collect evidence, consult students, teachers and parents, and advise ministers on further action. The paper says the taskforce will provide preliminary advice by mid-2027 and conclude its work by the end of 2027, unless Education Ministers determine otherwise. The agreed list also says the taskforce will advise ministers on further actions next year.

Ministers agreed the Year 5 NAPLAN writing assessment would return to handwritten completion in 2028, subject to further advice from ACARA on feasibility, costs and workload. ACARA is also to advise on handwritten NAPLAN writing for Years 7 and 9.

The paper recaps the Australian Framework for Generative Artificial Intelligence in Schools (National AI in Schools Taskforce, released late 2023, reviewed in 2024, review endorsed by Education Ministers in June 2025) and Education Services Australia product standards for generative AI.

Education Ministers agreed to restrict generative AI use by primary students and in secondary assessments, with each jurisdiction or sector setting timing, scope and application. They also agreed screen-use limits, a Digital Detox Taskforce to the end of 2027, and a return of Year 5 NAPLAN writing to handwriting in 2028 subject to ACARA advice.

proposedRecord.title: Australian Framework for Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Schools
proposedRecord.description: National framework guiding responsible and ethical use of generative AI in Australian schools. Education Ministers approved it on 5 October 2023; the department published it on 1 December 2023. Ministers endorsed the 2024 review in June 2025.
proposedRecord.content:
The Australian Framework for Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Schools guides responsible and ethical use of generative AI in school education. The Department of Education resource page says it supports school leaders, teachers, support staff, service providers, parents, guardians, students and policy makers.

The department announcement of the framework, published 1 December 2023, says Education Ministers approved it on 5 October 2023. It names six principles: Teaching and Learning; Human and Social Wellbeing; Transparency; Fairness; Accountability; and Privacy, Security and Safety. It says implementation is from Term 1 2024, and that the National AI in Schools Taskforce developed it with the Commonwealth, jurisdictions, school sectors and the national agencies (ESA, ACARA, AITSL and AERO).

The resource page states that in June 2025 Education Ministers endorsed the 2024 Framework Review, undertaken by the National AI in Schools Taskforce with jurisdictions, school sectors and national agencies. The page links a PDF and DOCX of the framework, a resource poster, and the 2024 review. This staging does not transcribe those files; they were not retrieved as bytes.

The release says the review makes 18 recommendations, including mandatory AI company reporting of misaligned behaviour or cyber incidents; consideration of criminal-law reform for serious misconduct; greater engagement with international counterparts and frontier AI developers; and strengthening resilience and response to AI incidents, including information sharing and cyber security. The recommendations page lists all 18. No separate recommendations PDF was linked from the Prime Minister's release or the PM&C recommendations page on 10 November 2026; the resource page is the recommendations text. The review was announced on 24 September 2026, when PM&C published terms of reference (https://www.pmc.gov.au/resources/terms-reference-rapid-review-australian-government-arrangements-ai-driven-cyber-incident). The 10 November release says the review was undertaken by PM&C in collaboration with the National Cyber Security Coordinator, the Office of AI, the Australian Signals Directorate, the Australian AI Safety Institute and Services Australia. The review page still describes the review as examining whether legislative, governance and information-sharing arrangements are fit for purpose, and its Recommendations section is dated 10 November 2026. This record is the completed rapid review and its published recommendations. It is not an enacted law. The same day's separate announcement that the Government will legislate mandatory safety and security protections for frontier AI companies is recorded as australian-ai-standards-frontier-safety-obligations-2026. source.title: New Australian AI safety and security protections
source.publisher: Prime Minister of Australia

agencies: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
Department of Industry, Science and Resources
proposedRecord.content: On 10 November 2026 the Prime Minister, the Deputy Prime Minister, the Minister for Home Affairs and Cyber Security and the Minister for Industry and Innovation announced that the Government will legislate mandatory artificial intelligence safety and security protections for all frontier AI companies that wish to operate in Australia, through Australian AI Standards legislation (https://www.pm.gov.au/media/new-australian-ai-safety-and-security-protections). The release says the protections would be enforced by a new targeted regulator for AI safety, working with the Australian AI Safety Institute, and that the regulator would be able to enforce significant penalties. It says companies will be required to: maintain security controls across all stages of development and deployment; identify and manage serious risks associated with their models; allow independent evaluation of their models; provide mandatory notification of incidents to the Australian Government rapidly; maintain and publish safety and security frameworks; and respond to updated standards and rules as technologies change. The release says these protections align with interim report recommendations from the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence, and that further details of the legislation will become available in due course. No bill, exposure draft or commencement date is published on this page. This is a separate announcement from the same day's release of the rapid review recommendations (pmc-rapid-review-ai-driven-cyber-incident-2026). It is not the 15 July 2026 announcement of Australian AI Standards for large AI data centres and the Office of AI (timeline event tl-2026-07-15-australian-ai-standards-office-of-ai), and there is no existing register record for the Australian AI Standards legislation to attach it to.

proposedRecord.title: ASD Blueprint for Secure Cloud — Artificial intelligence usage policy requirement
proposedRecord.description: ASD's Blueprint for Secure Cloud, first released on 19 December 2023, surfaces an artificial intelligence usage policy as an organisational policy expected under ISM control ISM-2074.
proposedRecord.content: ASD's Blueprint for Secure Cloud was initially launched on 19 December 2023. The Blueprint is maintained as a living resource; its change log does not record a change specific to this policy. It is better-practice guidance for designing, configuring and deploying secure cloud and hybrid workspaces, with a current focus on Microsoft 365. Its security and governance section links system security planning, the Essential Eight, system security plan annexes, and organisational policies and strategies. The organisational policies checklist explicitly identifies a general-purpose artificial intelligence usage policy as a requirement of ISM control ISM-2074. The Blueprint does not provide a template for this artefact, but positions it as part of the documentation agencies should review, develop and maintain when operating systems built using the Blueprint. ASD Essentials, launched on 15 October 2026, is the transition path from the Essential Eight; ASD keeps the Essential Eight on cyber.gov.au during the transition.

reviewedDate.notes: The consultation hub page states "Opened 31 Aug 2026" and "Closed 18 Sep 2026" as visible text, not as page metadata. The Attorney-General's media release of 31 August 2026 (https://ministers.ag.gov.au/media-centre/modernising-australias-privacy-laws-digital-age-31-08-2026) says the consultation paper and draft legislation were released that day.

proposedRecord.content: On 31 August 2026 the Attorney-General announced the release of a consultation paper and draft legislation to modernise Australia's privacy laws. The Attorney-General's Department consultation hub lists the consultation as opened on 31 August 2026 and closed on 18 September 2026. It publishes the Exposure Draft Privacy Amendment (Personal Data Protection) Bill 2026 and a Consultation Paper. The department says the reforms will bolster privacy protections and help tackle emerging risks from new technologies, including artificial intelligence and wearable devices such as smart glasses, and that the Bill remains subject to further consideration by government. The minister's release lists the key measures: a fair and reasonable test for collecting and using personal information; a right to erasure against large digital platforms; stronger standards for consent; and limits on trading in personal information without clear permission. It says AI-powered tools and devices, such as connected vehicles that continuously collect and process personal information, amplify privacy risks. The reforms build on the Privacy Act Review and the Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024 (register id federal-privacy-and-other-legislation-amendment-act-2024) and follow the Government Response to the Privacy Act Review Report (register id government-response-privacy-act-review-report). The Bill had not been introduced to Parliament when this record was staged.

proposedRecord.content: On 12 November 2026 the Minister for Employment and Workplace Relations, Amanda Rishworth, released the draft Best Practice Guide on the Adoption of AI in the Workplace (https://ministers.dewr.gov.au/rishworth/draft-best-practice-guide-ai-adoption-workplace-released). The release describes it as a guide focused on collaborative workplace transformation, developed through roundtables and forums with unions, employer peak representatives, academics, small businesses and large employers. It says the guide is underpinned by three themes, Plan, Enable and Embed, and sets out eight principles: capturing the opportunity; identifying use cases and assessing workplace readiness; cooperative planning and worker engagement; designing work and jobs; building capability; managing workforce transformation; establishing AI governance; and proactively managing risks and work health and safety. The release says each business will adapt the guide to its circumstances; it does not describe the guide as imposing obligations. The draft is open for public consultation through the department's consultation hub (https://consultations.dewr.gov.au/adopting-ai-in-the-workplace-best-practice-guide-draft) until 27 January 2027, per the release. The guide document itself was not read for this draft; the consultation hub page did not render for automated fetches.
